subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, April 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley for the second reading of Bill No. 104, to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Fleming.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to give my ruling on the point of order raised last night by the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming).
There is before the house a motion for the second reading of Bill No. 104, to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war. To this Mr. Fleming, member for Eglinton, moved in amendment:
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"While recognizing that the said bill deals with some matters such as old age pensions and veterans in the civil service which do not depend for constitutional validity on the existence of an emergency and some other matters which can only be dealt with by this parliament on the basis of an existing or apprehended emergency; and while willing to support properly drafted legislation dealing with such matters;
This house is unalterably opposed to the enactment of a measure to continue indiscriminately. the sweeping powers of the presently existing boards outside the control of parliament."
The first paragraph of this amendment is only a recognition in general terms of some matters dealt with in the bill; it purposes to place the house on record as recognizing that the bill deals with some matters and being prepared to support properly drafted legislation respecting such matters. The house can only make such recognition by voting partly for and partly against the bill, which is a meaningless proposition.
As to the house's readiness to support properly drafted legislation dealing with these matters, this is a question which will have to be submitted to the committee on the bill. Questions of drafting provisions are dealt with at that place and not with the Speaker in the chair.

As to the last paragraph of the amendment which declares that "the house is unalterably opposed to the enactment of a measure to continue indiscriminately the sweeping powers of the presently existing boards outside the control of parliament", it is merely asking that the house either approve or disapprove questions in indefinite terms. There is no doubt in my mind that proposals submitted for approval or disapproval must be set forth in expressed words, which can only be done in committee on the bill.
It happens that there are many orders and regulations included in this measure. There is a principle to each of them. Which of them the house should approve or disapprove is a mater which certainly is not covered by the amendment.
On the 24th of April, 1934, the Speaker of the house rejected an amendment proposed by the then leader of the opposition, which read as follows:
... . this house, while prepared to support legislation for assisting the orderly marketing of natural products, is unalterably opposed to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation, and which confers upon a minister of the crown and upon the governor in council unprecedented authority and unusual powers to restrict production, and interprovineial, interimperial and foreign trade as regards both exports and imports, as well as other autocratic powers.
In giving his decision against this amendment the Hon. George Black, then Speaker of the house, made the following statement:
The Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King in moving the amendment quoted paragraph 755 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, which paragraph is published as a quotation from May, 13th edition, at page 390, which is repeated by Bourinot at page 509:
"It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from the principles, policy or provisions of the bill."
This rule is subject to certain limitations. If the right hon. member had continued to quote from May, he would have found the following reference to an amendment to a motion for second reading of a bill:
"Nor may such an amendment deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto, which may be moved in committee-"
May, 13th edition, page 391. The precedent cited in May in support of this is found in 188 Parliamentary Debates, 4th series, column 76, The Education (Scotland) bill.
Mr. Speaker:	I have to rule that the amendment standing in the name of the hon. member for Glasgow and Aberdeen universities to the effect that the house while welcoming eduea-

Emergency Powers
tional legislation for Scotland regrets that the present measure does not propose change in the educational areas, which is urgently required in the interests of efficient administration-is not technically in order, because it does not challenge the principle of the bill. The question raised can he decided by an amendment to the bill itself. If the hon. member wants to object to the second reading, he should move that the bill be read this day six months.
An appeal was taken and the decision sustained by a vote of 103 to 52. This is a decision of the house itself which is equivalent to a standing order and must be adhered to. I therefore rule the amendment out of order.

I am not concerned with getting it in Hansard; I am concerned about checking the memories of hon. members opposite in connection with a lot of the promises they made during the six years this country was at war. I think the time that I will take this afternoon will be well spent because I still believe that some of them have consciences even though they have bad memories.
The matter now before the house is the principle of the bill we are now considering. That question is whether controls should be maintained in this country. I am going to take up some time this afternoon for the purpose of dealing with the principle of this
[Mr. Speaker.)
bill; the mechanical details can be discussed when we are in committee, but the broad principles upon which the bill is or should be based cannot be discussed at that time. I consider, Mr. Speaker, that any time spent by this house, no matter how long it may be, in clarifying the subject matter of this bill will be time well spent, because the very principles are involved for which we fought through six years of war and sacrificed a great many of the boys of this country.
Although there are several different groups in this house debate on the bill now before us divides the house into two. The Progressive Conservative party, the Liberal party and the Social Credit party all through this debate have stated in no uncertain terms that they believe in the system of free enterprise. The group to which I belong say that they do not, but rather that they believe in a planned order of society. That places the question squarely before the house. On this subject there are only two opinions.
Let me remind some of my free enterprisers in this house that the system of free enterprise has failed us twice in one lifetime and brought about armed conflict throughout the world.

speechtext: No.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I knew I would get under somebody's skin. Throw a stone into a pack of wolves and you will hit one and it will howl. I said that I was going to try to reawaken the conscience of the members of this house, because I still believe that they have a conscience. The fact that interruptions are coming so freely shows that I was not wrong in my surmise that they still have a conscience, and it is beginning to prick them.
I have said that that order of society brought on two wars in our lifetime, and it did. You cannot deny it.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: History proves it. I want to remind hon. gentlemen to my left who still believe in the free enterprise system, and who in the province of Alberta at the present time are administering a kind of economy that is evidently quite satisfactory to the Tory party-

speechtext:
The Tory party in Alberta decided that they would not contest the province, that they had a government that was satisfactory to them.
The lessons, Mr. Speaker, that we have to learn from the last war are, first, that the system of free enterprise did not measure up. Dictators were born and bred out of selfish-

Emergency Powers
ness and jungle law. That is the system of free enterprise. We aim to replace that kind of society by planning. There is not a member of this house who does not plan his own life, or at least he should. You plan your home.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would remind hon. members that they should not interrupt the hon. member who has the floor. A question may be asked with his permission.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do not mind the interruptions. It shows that I am beginning to hurt someone; I am saying something that is effective. If hon. members were reading their newspapers and paying no attention to me I would think that perhaps I was wasting my time, but I thank you, just the same, Mr. Speaker, for your assistance
I am surprised that prominent lawyers in this house who believe in the rule of law, just as we all do, and emphasize it earnestly at all times, will stand up in this house and oppose a bill which simply aims at bringing the rule of law into our economic life to replace gangsterism-and I use the word advisedly. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) yesterday placed clearly on the record of this house the fact that large corporations and companies in this country are running rampant in extracting from the people profits which no legal mind in this house could justify under present economic conditions. That is the first point I want to drive home-that we want to replace in our economic life tooth-and-claw law of the jungle with the rule of law as it exists in every other section of our society. We want a regulated order of society in which every person may have the opportunity to protect himself and his means of livelihood against unscrupulous people who want to exploit him and anyone who opposes this bill opposes that very principle.
I would remind my hon. friend who upholds the Social Credit-Tory coalition in Alberta that there were no controls in the thirties. We fought the 1914-18 war on the same slogans as those that were used in the last war. They were written by the same people. They were freedom, democracy, the right to live, homes for everyone. We came back after the 1914-18 war, and what did we find? There were no controls in the thirties except section 98 of the criminal code to control the worker, the fellow who died for you on the battlefields. When his fellow workers came back and asked you to live up to some of the promises you had made at that time, that was the kind of control they got. It was a form of control that was satisfactory to the wrong people. From 1930
to 1939 there was no government regulation of our economic affairs, and in that period we had a million and a half people unemployed and slave camps established in this country. That was a form of control that relegated to slave camps at 20 cents a day, where they were regulated and regimented, hundreds of thousands of people who had offered their lives to maintain democracy. Tear gas and the mounted police were used against them. That was a form of control in the wrong direction. Was there any freedom there? Freedom to go barefoot when you had no shoes; freedom to go hungry when you had nothing to eat; freedom to march from Vancouver to Ottawa to plead with those who sit in these great legislative chambers. No one objected to these controls except a few people like ourselves who were fighting them.
We have finished another war. I have listened in this house to many members who have expressed a fear of communism, but as I have said, the system of free enterprise has failed us twice in one lifetime, and the same seeds are being sown in this country today to defeat the ends for which we fought the last war. Again we promised the boys, the sons of the fathers to whom we made promises from 1914 to 1918, that they would come back to homes, to a new order of society; that the government would see to it that they were protected; that they would not go through the misery and degradation they experienced in the thirties. Twice in a lifetime we have given free enterprise all the rope it wanted, when it hanged and strangled the world, and we have signs enough on the North American continent to induce us to try to avert the conditions that may ensue; otherwise what happened in Europe and elsewhere will happen to us. Do not let us forget for a minute, when the country expresses fears of communism, that Karl Marx said a long time ago that capitalism had within itself the seeds of its own destruction. It will destroy itself if you leave it alone, if you give it enough rope and let it go.
We have done that twice in a lifetime, and capitalism has been destroyed in every part of the world except on the North American continent. Revolution, fascism and all the other isms about which we express fears are not common to any particular people. They are the product of a system, and we shall travel the same road if we allow that system unchanged, to prevail in the same way. Surely we have had enough lessons to take the abuses out of the system, the abuses that have destroyed the system throughout the world. This can be done only by removing fear, insecurity
Emergency Powers

and all the other factors that contribute to the destruction of confidence in the minds of the people.
We cannot do much about it so far as the United States is concerned. The picture there is not so bright. We can do something about it, however, in Canada. If free enterprise is capable of doing the job, why is it that the system functions and establishes standards of living for the workers of the world only when there is a war on, when most of the young and productive people are in the armed services? Then we can pay them wages and allowances, provide pensions, provide hospitals and the best of medical services and all that kind of thing. We can do that during a war, but when these people come back to the country they come back to a different set of conditions. Notwithstanding that there are plenty of resources, plant and machinery, we relegate them once more to the street.
Why is this? It is because of lack of planning. The Conservative party does not believe in planning, except from Bay street in Toronto and Jesse James street in Montreal. They are on record as being favourable to that, and we know what to expect from it. As soon as the war was over, up went the not-wanted signs again.
I am really ashamed to say in this house what the conditions are in the maritime provinces. Listening to a newscast this morning we heard that there were over 30,000 unemployed in the maritimes. On that little island that I come from there are 2,200 exservicemen, most of whom never had a job in their lives before they went into the services. They were unemployed under free enterprise. They donned the uniform and offered their lives for the institutions of the country, and they came back after all these promises that were made them. But, as I say, on that little island alone there are 2,200 of these men who today are unemployed, and they write pathetic letters, as the Minister of Veterans Affairs knows.
There is no work. Everything that was functioning during the war has been closed up. Back to the streets they go. I want to say for the benefit of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) that there is a strike on there at the present time, and I want to put a question to my hon. friends over here, and over there too, because I think there are a lot of Tories over there. I want to ask if they can tell me that the coal industry in the maritime provinces is better off because of the removal of controls.

For thirty years I worked in and around that industry and witnessed the most terrible conditions, socially, underground, and from every other point of view, and the most terrible relations with the employer, because we have the toughest octopus to grapple with in Canada in Dosco-tougher than any other organization in the country. There are no human values whatsoever so far as the management or the directorate of that organization is concerned.
During this war, with the establishment of national control in that industry, there was a different condition. I say without fear of contradiction, that the establishment of a national labour relations board, which took the whole industry and centralized it in Ottawa meant that, for the first time in my life or in my experience in that industry, we got away from Dosco's machine. Demands were made, the national board met with the Minister of Reconstruction, who handled the industry practically all through the war, and there were no strikes, no difficulties; wages were stepped up to some extent,; vacations with pay was established, and people in that part of the country were beginning to want to live.
In December, 1946, the federal government removed these controls and passed them back to the provincial government, and when you pass them back to the provincial government you pass complete control back to an agency of that corporation. That is all they are, an agency of the corporation. The executive board of the mine workers' union tried to work out an agreement, but there was no agreement-you cannot come into Ottawa; the controls are off. No more subsidies; we have to get back to free enterprise and give them the right to run the show themselves.
Well, they have run that show for a long time. The price of coal in this province has gone up approximately $3 a ton because of the removal of subsidies. That industry cannot pay wages in Nova Scotia because of the removal of production subsidies and the assistance the corporation was getting. I am not saying they were entitled to all the assistance they extracted from the government, but I say that was because this government lacked the machinery to scrutinize and check reports and balance sheets of the twenty-six subsidiary organizations by which that company can juggle costs around. It is pretty hard to chase them unless you are there all the time. Unless the federal government steps into the picture and takes that strike out of the hands of the provincial and local authorities, and reestablishes some kind of machinery in

Emergency Powers
Ottawa to settle it, the province of Nova Scotia will be depleted in a very short time. Hundreds of men who were in that industry during this war are leaving Nova Scotia and seeking work in other parts of Canada, because apparently no one is trying to do anything' in the way of settling that strike.
i mention this merely because I want to drive home the point of controls. It all adds up to public responsibility. When a member is elected to the House of Commons, or a government is formed, the people who send that member here or delegate power to the government expect that government to give them leadership and to supervise, the economy of the country and see that everyone is guaranteed the right to live in the country, that someone does not make a million dollars while another is on relief. That is their job, and when I hear some of our provincial people who believe in retaining provincial autonomy talking, they have been overseers of the poor for thirty years. That is all they are. There has been no government in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island. They want to hang on to something that exalts themselves. It is that vanity of man again, wanting to hang on to a little bit of power for himself.
I would never try to defend our provincial premier about the bickering and squabbling that he goes on with in this matter of provincial rights. This is where the power rests. There must be some central direction, and the people of Nova Scotia under the federal proposals would have been a hundred per cent better off than they could be in dealing with that little ox-cart government down there. I strongly urge what I suggested before to the Minister of Reconstruction-and I have a great deal of respect for him, too. There must be a great many Tories over there who keep him back, because I think that as an engineer and a practical man he knows the problem and wants to get things done, never mind the money. That is the proper attitude. There is something over there holding him back or he would have settled that strike, provided the necessary subsidies or got some kind of machinery in action. I suggest to him that he try to get together with the Minister of Labour and come to some understanding. It looks bad to see this situation: the Minister of Reconstruction makes a statement in the house to the effect-I think this was on April 1-that he was prepared to sit down with the industry and the union and work out some kind of subsidy arrangement by which that matter might be settled.

speechtext: That was April Fool's day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The date of your amendment.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Regardless of what date it was, the statement was made publicly and officially by a member of the cabinet. Then a few days later there is a statement from the Department of Labour-not from the minister but from some of his officials-to the effect that no subsidies will be provided to clean up that problem in Nova Scotia. I suggest that they get together.
I am not sure that my friends to my right or their coalition on our extreme left can stand up in this house and tell me that the coal industry, the steel industry, the shipping industry, the fishing industry, or the textile industry-all basic industries in this country-are better off today than they were during this war when the government were planning production, allocating materials, and supervising the general income of the country. There is no comparison. If it could be done in time of war, there is no reason why it should not be a hundred per cent easier to do it in time of peace. I cannot understand it. I would advise my Conservative friends over there to do a little checking up. They are venomous on this matter of controls and free enterprise. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker)-I am sorry he is not here now -is a man for whom I have a great deal of respect. He is a lawyer, a good reasoner, and logical in practically everything except where he sits. On this matter of controls he gave the Conservative party some very good advice back in 1942. Speaking at the business men's club in Toronto, he said this:
No one can successfully argue that principles of the Victorian era can cope with the conditions in times that produce Sir Stafford Cripps, (a socialist) as deputy prime minister (of Britain), and William Temple as Archbishop of Canterbury.
He goes on to tell about that kind of thing, but the meat of his remarks is farther down, where he says, "Bureaucracy is danger". The article reads:
Mr. Diefenbaker said the danger exists of government by bureaucracy after the war.
"The Liberal party today stands for reaction, the C.C.F. for complete nationalization, which will destroy private enterprise," he said. "The Conservative party must meet this challenge that comes to it and show the people that our economic system shall continue to be one of free enterprise under stringent control . . ."
The caption of the article was "Advises Tories to Modernize".

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
How could the Tories modernize?
Emergency Powers

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That was in 1942. They did modernize to this extent: the word "progressive" is a modem term, and they adopted it on that advice.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Twenty years too late.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If you listen to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) or the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) or any member of this group, you may say: Those fellows are just propagating for their own cause-the socialist cause. But this advice was not given by a socialist, and it should be seriously taken.

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Propagation, you mean?

subtopic: COTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Certainly. That is the only way you can create things. Let me read a short statement by another person who is not a socialist. I heard the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) one evening quoting the Pope's encyclical. I do not believe in bringing religion into a discussion of this kind, because a man's religion is a matter between himself and his God. But I do say this. For nineteen hundred years we have been preaching Christianity and it is nearly time we began to put it into practice. We certainly have not been practising it, judging by conditions in the world for the last fifty years at least. I am going to quote Monsignor J. A. Ryan, National Catholic Welfare Conference. This is a statement he made in 1943 and I would advise the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) to listen carefully:
Unless the middle classes-that is, the comfortable farmers, the members of the professions, the small business men, the holders of executive and directive positions in the great corporations, and indeed the majority of the "white collar" classes-cease to get their opinions from the daily papers and strive to acquire a greater amount of realistic economic intelligence, they (the middle classes) may exercise sufficient voting power to place the champions of "free enterprise" in control of economic reconstruction after the war. From such a calamity, may the Good Lord deliver us.
That is not from a socialist. That is from a person who is realistic, and who learned a lesson from the last two wars.
While we know where the Conservatives stand in this matter of controls and the planned economy, we are doubtful about where the present government stands, because since the termination of the war they have paid lip service to controls, have spoken of trying to avoid exploitation, and all that kind of stuff; and I think most of the people who make those statements really mean them at the time. But we have been watching. The cost of living is going up. No public works 
programme of any kind has been instituted. Practically all the war assets built up by the people during the war have been scrapped without being put to productive use. The ranks of the unemployed are beginning to swell. There are rumblings from the farmer, the industrial worker and the white collar worker, who I think perhaps has suffered a worse squeeze than either the farmer or the worker, from the standpoint of taxes, because he is in between, on a fixed salary, and has had to take the squeeze from both sides. That cannot continue for very long without a smash-up of some kind. I want to say in all sincerity that perhaps in 1939 Hitler saved us from a revolution on this continent. If any serious minded person will look back at the conditions which existed in 1938 and 1939 right across Canada and throughout the United States he will realize that had they lasted for another six months without a bust-up of some kind we would have had serious internal disturbances in this country. We do not want a set-back now which would allow that sort of thing to develop again.
There is only one way to avoid that. We have two alternatives, either to go to war or to create employment. The people of this country do not expect too much. They want jobs; they want houses. They are quite prepared to work for them and produce. They do not want charity; they do not want handouts. They want to live as decent citizens, and they have that right. Those were the promises we made them while we were fighting the war. Personally I am ashamed of the conditions that exist in the part of the country from which I come. They should not exist, and they could have been avoided if the government had accepted its responsibility. Only yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) definitely stated that all the subsidies were coming off. When you knock off the subsidies under this form of society you destroy price ceilings. You cannot hold down prices without subsidies unless you have in the field an army of policemen checking everything that is sold. But you can hold' down prices and redistribute income by means of subsidies. They are not appreciable to every industry; in many cases they are not necessary, but they are necessary in some of the basic industries, and should be continued. When the Minister of Finance, speaking for the government, makes the statement that they have officially decided to discontinue the subsidy arrangements, then he tells us there is no longer any desire on the part of the government to manage the economy of the country, because it can only be done in that way under this form of society.

Emergency Powers
I am coming to the end of my time, Mr. Speaker. I could inject many matters into this discussion. I hope some member of the cabinet will speak before this debate is con-, eluded, and I should like him to answer two or three questions; I think it is necessary at this time. In its issue of April 12, 1947, the Montreal Gazette carried a story from Ottawa that the government is carefully scrutinizing price increases arising out of the recent release from control of thousands of goods and services, and will move without delay to reimpose price ceilings in any case where the increase appears to be unreasonable or exorbitant. I should like some member of the cabinet, if and when he speaks, to tell us if that is really government policy. If so, what checks are they maintaining on the situation? Why has no action been taken so far in connection with such items as newsprint? These are three questions on which I think the Canadian people, and particularly members of this house, want some reassurance.
In conclusion I want to repeat what I said when I started, that as far as I can see there are only two opinions in this house on this question of free enterprise as opposed to a managed economy. As I see it, the attitude in all corners of the house is opposed to the attitude taken by this party. Our policy is clear-cut. There is no equivocation when we say that if we were in power we would establish a managed or planned economy in this country. We would go to the mat with anyone extracting more than his share of the national income, and would see to it that everyone was provided with a means of life. Is it not startling to realize that in a country such as this a large section of the population cannot get-enough to eat?

Mr. DAVID A. CROLL (Spadina): Mr. Speaker, the Easter vacation and the decontrol measures taken before and during that time gave all of us an unusual opportunity not only to feel the pulse of our constituencies but actually to take stock. The people I met during that time were greatly disturbed about our decontrol measures. I met people in all walks of life, and found the same complaint on every side. Somehow or other they got the impression that we in this house do not realize that laissez-faire is dead and buried. There are still some who believe there are hon. members in the house who feel that the good old days ought to be brought back-the good old days of no government intervention, the good old days of the thirties, when we had the complete freedom of action which brought false booms and real depressions.
Many people have a different understanding of free enterprise and laissez-faire. To me it means that if business is left alone it will work in such a manner as to bring about ideal economic conditions for the average man. Yet it overlooks one important truism, that industry is based upon the profit motive. While I have nothing against the profit motive as such, there are times when there is a clash between the justifiable interests of the business man and those of the consumer. Under those conditions the function of government is to act as a brake, when industry, so to speak, tries to run away with itself. In other words there will be times when controls are not only desirable but essential; and, so far we in this country have no complaint. Controls have not failed us, nor have they been the cause of shortages. During the war the government used successfully the device of controls to divert the tremendous output of industry to the interests of the state-which at that time was the fullest prosecution of the war. Now in these critical and emergent years of peace we must take these same forces and use them, but not, as some political thinkers would suggest, to bring industry back to normal. To my mind that is a label only, and one which hides a multitude of iniquities. As we saw in the thirties, in the titanic struggle of economic forces the small man was crushed.
The outstanding economic factor in our economy today is scarcity. So long as economic scarcity is with us, industry can use it to achieve its own gains. After all, it is not the function of either the landlord or the mill owner to run his business for the benefit of the public. The true function, as they see it, is to produce profits; and it would be naive for us to assume otherwise, or to ask them to run their business in an altruistic manner. The
;Ur. Gillis.l
good business man is not operating for the sake of charity; and if scarcity presents him with an opportunity, he takes advantage of it. If for instance, there is greater promise of gain from building glamorous moving picture theatres or elaborate night clubs rather than houses, how many business men would forgo the greater profit for the greater need? But it is only by the will of the people as expressed through parliament that we can force industry to work for the common good as well as for its own good.
As I see it therefore, so long as the element of scarcity prevails-and none of us can predict how long that will be-we dare not decontrol too fast. And that we are doing at the present time. In normal times there was always a check of monopolistic tendencies within a healthy business organism by what economists call the marginal producer, the man who was ready to compete at a small rate of profit. But today, when goods are scarce, there is no incentive for such marginal production. We have on the one hand a great shortage of commodities at home and abroad, and on the other hand a comparative abundance of money, although the situation at the present time is tighter than it was a year ago, as many businessmen will agree. In an uncontrolled economy what is the result? Demand forces prices up. Previous wage scales become obsolete with the rising cost of living, and you have the whole inflationary spiral of skyrocketing prices and costs which can only end in disaster.
There is a remedy; there is an alternative, and that alternative is controls. If the situation is not too far gone-and it is not in this instance-and if business men are prepared to work together for the good of the country and their own good, then we can rely on industry to control itself without any need for government intervention. So far it must be admitted that industry has not done a good job of self-control. I have only to ask the house to refer to the speech delivered yesterday by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Cold-well) in which he quoted figures giving some indication of the abnormal profits of corporations. I picked up the Globe and Mail of April 12 and on the financial page I found the following headlines:
Zeller's sales and profits hit a fifteen year peak.
St. Regis Paper sets new record.
Hiram Walker profits up 58-7 per cent Consolidated Bakeries lifts profit 22 cents share. Gurney Foundry profit is $6.46 against $2.08.
Atlas Steels earns 96 cents against 61.
And on and on, all in the one day. Then
I recall reading a report on the same page

Emergency Powers
that a movie corporation had had the highest earnings in the history of the company, yet admission prices were raised throughout the length and breadth of this country. Are these indications that the Canadian business man is waking up to his responsibilities? Frankly I do not think he is. Despite what I have said about the profit motive and private enterprise I think the average business man has enough common sense and enough patriotism to impose his own controls once he becomes fully aware of the dangers inherent in a runaway situation. The words uttered yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) are reported in the Montreal Gazette of this morning, and he is reported as saying that the government would reimpose controls in any case where it was felt that the public was being exploited.
It is well for the house to know that some time ago jute bags were decontrolled. There were none on the market; they were not available, but within forty-eight hours after the order came into effect they were available at double the previous price. The government immediately reimposed the control, and today they can be bought at a reasonable price.
In referring to the business man I am not talking about the fly-by-night.ers who come up from nowhere on the strength of a few quick killings. I am thinking of the firms who were here ten and twenty years ago and who will still be here ten and twenty years from now when the quick-profit boys are dead and gone. They are the ones who have everything to gain from a policy of control and self-control until such time as we level out our economy and the normal checks and balances of a free economic society can come into play.
I conceive then of decontrol as neither a quick process of throwing the book out the window and going back to business as usual, nor a long-drawn-out process of hanging on to a horde of irksome regulations until that elusive will-o'-the-wisp called normalcy returns. Precipitous decontrol will start us down the primrose path of higher prices with consequent consumer resistance, wage demands and the inevitable strikes and unemployment with ultimate frustration. By our haste I believe that we will defeat the very purpose we are setting out to achieve. The time has come for the government to stop decontrolling and to reexamine the position of the articles or commodities that have been decontrolled.
During the war years we took away, in whole or in part, some of the most cherished prerogatives of private industry. We told industry what to produce, how much to produce and how much profit to make. If we had not, perhaps industry would have made a great 83166-132
deal more money than it actually did; although I would say in passing that when you recall that last year Canadian corporations realized net profits after taxation of half a billion dollars one is forced to the conclusion that industry has not done badly under controls. Bj' its present conduct capital, which has the most to gain from the free enterprise system, is fouling its own nest by exacting the large and abnormal profits that have been referred to in this house during the last few days.
I view decontrol as a process of letting controls go as quickly as is compatible with the welfare of the little man', to the point where government can hand the whole thing back to private enterprise and say, "You take it from here." A realization by business men of the heavy responsibilities that are theirs today will speed up this reconversion. The sooner they are prepared to exercise selfcontrol, the sooner will we be able to dispense with government control.
In the meantime, for the protection of everyone, a large measure of official control must remain. Our affirmative decision on this point will be met with approval by the little man throughout Canada. As for the comparatively few who will object-they are really a small minority, but they make a noise like a majority-I would say tnat they are guilty of selfish or illogical thinking. Let us give them the benefit of the doubt by saying that they are only illogical, and let us point out to them that those who oppose controls in principle or in fact are blindly evoking the attitudes of bygone years when planning and controls were linked with the totalitarianism of Germany and Italy.
Many of these people reason that Hitler and Mussolini imposed a controlled economy on their countries and that all kinds of evils followed as a natural result-loss of liberty, persecution, regimentation, mass murder, and war. They are convinced that if we hold on to the few controls that remain we shall be selling the freedom of this country down the river-quite overlooking the fact that Britain, probably the most largely controlled English speaking country in the world today, is also the one in which the flame of freedom burns the brightest. Only persons who have little faith in democracy should live in fear of democratic controls. People have come to take for granted the exercise of economic controls which prior to the war they would have called totalitarian. We must not forget that the little people of this country do not merely accept controls; they actually want them, and they do not want to go back to the days of false booms and real depressions.

Something has been said about planning. Corporations do not grow up like Topsy. They are planned, they are blue-printed. The better the plans, the better the corporation; the better the corporation, usually the better the plans. If it is a good thing for a corporation to plan, why is it not a good thing for the individual to plan? Why should not many individuals plan? Why not have the government plan for individuals? After all, planning is not the exclusive property of socialist or totalitarian countries; it is also a healthy ingredient of the new democracy. The little people are weak; they lack buying resistance. Their needs are immediate-food clothing, rent-and their bargaining capacity is weak. They know this and they look to parliament to plan for them. They remember well how we planned during the war and what a good job we did, and they look to us for a continuation of planning in the post-war period.
I believe that the people have always been in favour of controls and they call for the retention of essential controls. The uncertainty of life in an unbalanced economy makes this a "must" for the little man. The recently announced increase of ten per cent in rentals means an immediate rise in the cost of living, which is placing an unbearable burden on the shoulders of people who cannot take it. The low income group, the people on fixed incomes, the white-collar workers, are finding times in this country hard in the midst of the greatest corporation profits in our history. How do we justify it? How do we explain it? How do we reconcile it?
Labour made certain gains across the board last year in an attempt to bring their earnings into line with the then high cost of living. The gains they achieved did not put them ahead of the game-they only compensated for the years when wages were frozen and the cost of living got ahead of them. Last year's wage gains were not prospective- they were retroactive. They took up some of the slack between wages and prices as they were last summer, but they were not a cushion against rising prices in the future. In other words it was not a question of their gains being wiped out by the increased cost of living in the past year, they have actually lost ground, and once more the prices-wages equation is being tipped dangerously to their disadvantage.
I ask the members of this house to look to the south and take note of what is happening in the United States on the labour front. Let it not happen here. I know that the question uppermost in the minds of the mem-

bers of this house and the people of Canada is this: How long will our economy need the controlling hand of government? How quickly can that hand be relaxed? I confess, Mr. Speaker, I do not know the answer. I know that we cannot bring about decontrol on a fixed time-table. Conditions and events, not only in Canada but all over the world, have a direct bearing on the problem. If there is a strike in the motor industry in the United States it will be only a matter of three weeks before our factories are closed. If we are unfortunate enough to have a coal strike in the United States it will probably be only a month before our factories will feel it. Any large strike in the United States affects us economically almost as much as it does the state of Texas. And so we have to keep our eyes open. We cannot remove control on a fixed time-table. We must face the issue and see it clearly. The issue is not whether we should have controls or no controls. The problem for Canada is whether we should have more or fewer controls. Apart from the real need there is to hang on to some essential controls until we have levelled off our economy, the fact remains that people have tasted the benefits of a Canadian planned economy and are not going to give it up lightly. They like it.
The last decontrol order has had a disturbing effect. Today decontrol is unrealistic. With savings down from last year, with production and inventories up, with profits never higher in the history of this country, despite the ruin that was to come to us from last year's strikes with prices escalating, but up, and with labour straining but acting restrained, the time has come for a decision.
This debate on controls has been going on for weeks, and while we have been talking the government has been whittling away at the subject matter of our debate. The recent increase in rentals is a case in point. I should have liked to see the ten per cent increase in rentals made conditional on the landlord's renovating and repairing the premises, but there it is. Time is running out and I urge most strongly that we make up our minds now, while there is still something left to make up our minds about.

Mr. Speaker, I admit some guilt in the matter, but I do feel, since this matter has been introduced, that perhaps I should do something about it. Perhaps I would be permitted to answer the hon. member's question-it practically amounted to a question-and that done, I promise that I shall return to the business before the house. This is a report of a Social Credit convention and it states:	"Social Credit convention
attracts only three persons". Apparently Doctor Haideman was there, and there were two others. They did not admit the press, or there would have been four. As regards my hon. friend's question, it says that social crediters may cooperate with other parties. Doctor Haideman says they can do so if they desire-with, I presume, the qualification which my hon. friend has stated-provided that it is in the interests of the country. And after all, when three good men and true believe that, there must be something in it.
To come back to the question, or rather to initiate the question of controls, I am a believer in controls so long as I think the controls are, as my hon. friend has suggested, for the good of the country at large. There was a protest by certain women in this country not very long ago. a delegation of western women. I followed with some interest the eastern press comments on that delegation. The eastern press was practically unanimous in saying that the movement was communist-inspired. Perhaps it was to some extent, but I know for a fact that they were not all communists. However I would advise
Emergency Powers

the government, whethej' there be some truth in the suggestion or not, that they had better not take comfort from that fact or try to get behind it, because I think that, irrespective of' what people had given the delegation their blessing, their cause was supported by all the women of the country, if not vocally, at least in their hearts and minds.
The government's idea would seem to be that the release of controls does not necessarily mean an increase in prices. The theory which we have heard expounded time and again by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) is that the throwing off of controls will so stimulate production that supply will quickly equate demand and prices will level off. I do not think that assumption has proved to be valid in the experience of the United States, nor do I think it is valid in the light of our experience here. The minister himself, I believe, pointed out what had happened in the United States in the matter of an increase in prices when he was defending the idea of continued control, even if that continued control were only for a short period.
I would ask him whether, in his opinion, the removal of these ceilings has not been to some degree contributory to that result. I think the government's policy is most inconsistent in the matter. The Minister of Justice, when he rose in his place to introduce this legislation in its various stages, knew that he had to defend the policy of controls, a control which, it is true, he was asking only for the period of one year. But it had to be defended, and in defending it he gave some interesting information.
He said that during the war-I believe it was from 1942 to 1946-in each year of that period these controls had saved the consumers of the country a billion and a half dollars. I believe, although I did not check this, that someone said these controls had saved us about fifty-five dollars for each dollar they had cost us for their operation. We were told by the Minister of Justice and by other members on that side of the house that the too hasty abandonment of controls would produce chaos, and the minister warned us-this time the Minister of Justice himself, I believe -about the plight of the salaried worker, the white-collar man, the wage-earner, the pensioned person and so forth. And then, having traced the tremendous benefits that these controls had brought during the war, he said almost in the same breath, "Of course, it is our policy to get rid of the thing as soon as possible." I will admit there was a qualification. I am not quoting him, but he made the qualification, "as quickly as conditions permit". I say that in justice to him.
	1
My point is that the conditions do not yet permit, and that is evidenced by the steadily increasing prices of commodities in this country. Members of the cabinet have talked of orderly decontrol. I think it has ceased to be that, and has become decontrol in unholy haste. On the very day that the right hon. gentleman was advancing such eloquent arguments for the maintenance of certain price ceilings, and introducing price legislation which would preserve that maintenance, we find his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) cutting the ground from under the feet of such legislation by releasing numerous items from under these ceilings.
Going to my home at Easter time, I found that we were paying higher prices for simple little things, the things that aggravate the cost of living. I would bring this to the attention of the government, which is usually politically conscious. I do not see why it should be so freely butting its head against the wall of public opinion. We are paying eight cents for chocolate bars, and an increase of one cent a pound for sugar; we are threatened with a ten per cent increase in rents under certain conditions; there are increases in the price of tea, coffee, soap, fuel, shirts if you can get one, and all the rest of it; jams, shortening and practically everything else.
May I remind this usually astute government that everybody-rich or poor-is taking note of these things, and, in particular, of the cost of the things which I have mentioned, which comprise a great part of the purchases of those in the lower income brackets. The man in the higher salary brackets, who spends a lesser proportion of his income on living, is not much affected by the prices of these simple things, but to a great many other people they mean the difference between decent living and a stringent economy.
The government is, of course, aware of these things. I have here something put out by the government, by a publications bureau of some sort. The series is "Wartime Controls" by the wartime information board of Ottawa, September 12, 1944, in which this statement appears:
Uncontrolled inflation is a severe and unfair form of taxation. Under conditions of inflation, while some wages and salaries may keep pace with increases in prices, wages and salaries in general can never keep abreast of increases in the cost of living.
I think that is true. Wages are now lagging behind. The logical thing now is for another increase in wages to keep up with increased prices, and there we go in that famous old

Emergency Powers
merry-go-round to which a lack of planning apparently always leads. I continue the quotation:
For that section of the population living on pensions, annuities and other forms of small savings bringing in a fixed income, inflation spells disaster, poverty and hardship.
To continue with another clause in the same document:
Economic stabilization is necessary to protect the savings of the Canadian people. Most Canadians have saved something for the proverbial rainy day. They have put money into savings accounts, purchased insuran ;e policies, annuities and other types of fixed dollar investments (those which bring in the same number of dollars regardless of what they will buy).
Might I say that those dollars do not buy as much now as they did when those people invested them? I know, from experience with my own friends, that they are, little by little, step by step, withdrawing their savings from the bank, withdrawing their bonds and selling them in order to eke out their wages and salaries in an attempt-a temporary and perhaps foolish one-to preserve the standard of living which they had been accustomed to during the war.
I speak here in what I conceive to be the interests of the people of my constituency, and I fancy they are very much like the people in other constituencies. This is a burning question in my own city. It is the thing about which people are talking most. I noticed the other day in the report of the Gallup poll that right up at the top of the list of things about which the people are now concerned-I mean regarding government matters and legislation-is the item of the rising costs of the necessities of life. I found there was practically no disagreement among the people of all shades of opinion whom I represent, with the argument that I am advancing here today. I know that argument would not be advanced by everyone in this country. It would not be advanced by those who ordinarily get their excellent standard of living from selling goods to the Canadian people. I would not fancy, for instance, that the manufacturers would advocate such a policy. They tell us that increased prices are necessary to meet increased wages, expenses and so forth. If we were to examine that statement, aided by certain statistics, we would find what was advanced by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) yesterday, and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) advanced the same argument today, so I shall -not weary the house with a recital of the tremendously increased profits and dividends of these great companies and corporations for
the year 1946 as compared with the year 1945. But the figures are reliable. They were quoted, I think yesterday, from the Financial Post. I do not think these companies need any particular relief. They are doing quite nicely. And so this government-and I must say it, though reluctantly-by deliberate action, has increased the cost of living in such degree as it has abandoned the price ceiling. The government has, in so doing, ignored the protests of the people of this country, protests which have been expressed in many places and notably in this house, when one remembers the result of the vote at the last session on the question of the milk subsid\\ It has flouted the will of the people as expressed by parliament.
The fact is that wages and small salaries, even those which have been increased, cannot be stretched any farther to cover any increased cost of living. Yesterday, when the Minister of Finance made a statement I noticed that he said, "Let the law of supply and demand operate; we are going to get back to the position where the law of supply and demand will operate." Well, the truth is that the law of supply and demand is being more and more interfered with. One has only to read the report on cartels to prove that to his own satisfaction. Control is constantly and generally exercised; and this party would rather that it be exercised by a government composed of representatives of the people of the country than that it be exercised by those interests which are opposed to the interests of the great masses of the people and are interested, first of all-I shall not say altogether, but first of all-in their own gain. The Minister of Finance said that a wise industrialist would moderate his own profits voluntarily. Might I for a moment use the vernacular and say, "What a hope!" The days of benevolent despotism are over. I do not think a modern industrialist has the same ideas of benevolence as had the feudal barons. I think it is too much to hope. In the state of things as they are, is it sensible, since success is so generally measured in terms of money and power, that we can expect that from the modern industrialist? Nowadays the modem industrialist, when a concern does not pay, shuts it down and would like to throw his workers into the lap of a benevolent government. Those things have not been always so.
If I may digress here for a moment, I shall recall the case of a linen manufacturer who lived in the country I came from. That man was benevolent. He was not even a despot. He was the great man in that little country
Emergency Powers

place, and there were linen mills there. This was in the north of Ireland, and those hon. members who know the history of that country will know what the linen industry meant to that land for many years. Then the day came when the linen business began to go down. Women ceased to wear linen clothes. People ceased to use heavy linen tablecloths and the business began to deteriorate. This man had accumulated a certain amount of money and he had a very fine estate. He looked after two or three villages, and he Lad one or two mills. Things began to go bad. That man did not dismiss an employee. That was most uneconomic, our modern industrialist would say. Certain industrialists even then said that, but he refused to change his method. This had been his father's business before him. These were his people and he felt a certain responsibility for them. To make a long story short, I shall merely say that he kept that business running until he had mortgaged every stick of his own and until he himself was in the same condition, as far as wealth or the lack of it was concerned, as the people who worked for him. That type of benevolence is not very evident in the industrial .world today, nor would I reasonably expect that it should be. We think, of course, there is something that we could substitute for feudalism.
To conclude these few remarks, I would say simply that I am in favour of any scheme or any control which will preserve for the people of this country in time of peace at least the standard of living they attained during the war. While I am on my feet I should like in a word or two to express my ideas about this business of regulation, this business of freedom, this business of individual liberty. No man in his senses in this house would say that I or those around me believe in enslaving anybody, least of all ourselves. I believe men of good will have the same objects in view. I do not know of anyone in this group who does not value his personal liberty and freedom. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) rides this subject on almost every occasion, and if I might say so without being rude, rides it to death.
In my opinion a certain amount of regulation is necessary. To me freedom is not licence. To me some regulation is necessary, with the sole object that we may attain that freedom which all men desire. That is how I look at this subject, and I shall leave it at that.

With respect to the measure itself, as I have said it seeks to put into one statute some fifty-seven orders in council which were passed in time of war. The motion now before us is that the bill be given second reading. As hon. members know, an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), which amendment was declared by His Honour the Speaker to be out of order, so that we are now dealing with the main motion. We think it is a position in which the members of this house should not have been placed, a position where we have to support all these measures or to oppose them all. As a matter of fact we do not oppose some of them, but we do oppose others. And we oppose certain of the wide powers which, under this legislation, are left with officials. It is clear, therefore that, no matter how members vote, they are likely to be misrepresented with respect to certain sections of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has endeavoured to place before the house the position in which the members of his party find themselves with respect to this bill. I should like to say a few words about the position in which we of this group find ourselves. Unlike the leader of the opposition and his followers, it has been our intention right from the start to support the second reading of this bill, and from time to time we have so indicated. However I may say that we support the measure because we would not be satisfied with anything less at this stage in our country, but we are by no means satisfied with the extent to which it goes. In saying that, I have in mind the limitation placed in the bill upon the principle of price control, and also the fact that the bill gives the government power to revoke price control at any time in whole or in part, which is now happening from day to day. I also have in mind the views I have expressed repeatedly with regard to other matters covered in the bill, such as old age pensions. We are by no means satisfied with a bill that simply extends the present $25 for a period of time. We believe that long before this the government should have given us an opportunity to vote on its proposed amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act itself, and boost the pension to some reasonable amount. However though we are not satisfied with the extent to which the bill goes, we state quite clearly that this country could not get along with anything less, could not run the risk of the chaos that would ensue if this bill were not passed, and for that reason we intend to support it.
I want to say further, though, that we do not feel the house has yet had an opportunity to express itself clearly, by means of a vote, on the basic principle that is before us, so far as controls are concerned. There has been a good deal of arguing between hon. members on the government side and those in the official opposition; but in principle there is very little difference between them. Spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative party contend that controls should be brought to an end immediately. The position taken by most speakers on the Liberal side of the house is that controls should be brought to an end, but more slowly, and through what is called a programme of orderly decontrol. The only difference between those two positions is one of timing. Both agree that controls should come to an end, and that we should get back to what is called a free economy.
When we in this group refer sincerely to this talk of getting back to a free economy as a process of returning to what we had in the thirties, we are met with some rude interjections. We are told sometimes that we do not believe it ourselves, and that we are resorting to soap-box oratory, and that sort of thing. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is quite clearly what we are heading for, if we go back to what is called a free economy. To call it free does not make it free.
Freedom is one of the things in which, in principle, members on all sides of the house are united. We all believe in it firmly; we strive for it, and would do anything we could to protect the freedom of our citizens. But it does seem to me there is too little realization in the house of the fact that, if we are going to hold on to our political freedom and to the civil liberties we prize so much, we must move on and achieve a much wider measure of economic freedom-and not just for the few, but for all the people of this country. And that, to use a phrase the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) so frequently employs, means the rule of law. The contention of those of us in this group is that the rule of law must begin to take effect in the economic sphere. We contend that democracy is control by the people of the things that affect the people. Two or three generations ago economic processes did not greatly affect the individual lives of the people in the country. My grandfather, and his father and grandfather before him, eked out an existence in Shelburne county, Nova Scotia, planting potatoes among the rocks and doing a bit of fishing. Economic processes did not play a large part in their free-
Emergency Powers

dom. In that day freedom consisted in protection from inroads by the state or the government.
But times have greatly changed. Peoples' lives today, from the cradle to the grave, are affected by the economic processes which surround us. The most immediate evidence of that statement is the effect that the rising cost of living is having on the lives of our people at the present time. And I suggest that if we are to carry out the full meaning of democracy, the people who are elected to represent the interests of about 12,000,000 Canadians must see to it that in the name of the people they have control over the economic processes which affect those
12.000,00 people.
The point at which this is most evident is in the rising cost of living. As members of parliament, members of a democratic representative body, I submit we are negligent in our duty if we sit idly by and let the cost of living sky-rocket, and our people suffer as they will as a consequence.
That is the reason we have been contending, from the time this debate opened, that instead of presenting us with a measure which merely provides for the continuance of controls on a skeleton basis, just long enough to get rid of them, the government should be introducing a system of orderly and democratic controls so as to combat any inflationary tendencies, combat the rising cost of living, and make possible the achieving of greater justice and greater equality among our people.
The very fact that the leader of the opposition has indicated that he and his followers intend to vote against this measure, and that it is known that we intend to vote for it, shows what a confused situation confronts us.

I suggest that the real issue is not as to whether controls should come off today or next week, or even at some time within a year. The real issue is whether or not the parliament and government of this country, in the name of the people, are going to pursue a policy of orderly and democratic controls, in the belief that it is our democratic duty to protect the Canadian people by having something to say in their name about the economic processes which affect their lives.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I rise now' to present another amendment. This amendment is one that we have thought out carefully in the light of the experiences that we have had thus far in this debate. I mean, by that, that we have done our best to word it in such a way as to make sure that it will be in order. My hon. friends to my right moved an amendment on April 1, which, 1 grant, stated the issue as they see it. However, this afternoon that amendment was ruled out of order, in which ruling we of this group concurred. Yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldweil) moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply, which was ruled out of order on the ground that it anticipated doing things which could be done in committee on Bill No. 104.
We hope that the amendment we now propose to move will avoid that supposed error for it suggests something different that we feel should be done than what is now placed before us. In other words, it will suggest to the house that there should be introduced a system of orderly and democratic controls. I submit that that is quite different from a measure which provides merely for the continuation of certain skeleton powers until such time as they are revoked. Therefore I submit that the amendment which I shall offer in a moment cannot be ruled out of order as was the case with the one proposed yesterday.

That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the headlong decontrol policy of the government has depressed the standard of living of the people, threatens the country with economic chaos, and is surrendering the future of Canada to profiteering and monopoly;
And be it further resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to the introduction of a system of orderly and democratic controls and the restoration of lower prices for the necessities of life, particularly articles of food and clothing, soap and shortening, shelter, household appliances, and supplies and machinery needed in agriculture, in order to eliminate the injustices which now exist and to arrest the rapidly rising cost of living.
In drafting this amendment, we took into consideration citation 657 to be found on page 228 of Beauchesne, third edition, which says in part:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution . . .
And so on.
Then on page 337 of Beauchesne, third edition, will be found form No. 93, which gives the form for an amendment to the motion for the second reading of a bill. As I was about to indicate a few moments ago when Your Honour asked me to read my 83166-133
amendment, there have been two amendments in exactly this form moved this session. One was moved on February 21 and is recorded on page 697 of Hansard. That was an amendment which I made to the motion for the second reading of the redistribution bill; it asked that the bill be not given second reading at that time but that the house resolve a certain proposition. The other occasion was on March 31, as recorded on page 1910 of Hansard, when the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) moved an amendment to the second reading of the bill providing for the appointment of auditors for the Canadian National Railways. Again the amendment proposed that the bill be not then read a second time but that the house by resolution declare an alternative principle.
I have taken this much time to deal with the technical points in order to make clear how perfectly in order this kind of amendment is. As I indicated earlier, this kind of amendment has been moved twice this session, has been accepted by Your Honour and voted upon by this house. I submit that that is what this house wants, namely, an amendment which states the issue clearly so that we can vote upon it and let the country know where we stand. This amendment does not simply make decontrol a matter of time, which is the issue between the government and the opposition; it calls for a definite policy of orderly and democratic control; it calls for a permanent policy looking toward the exercise by parliament of its democratic responsibility to have something to say about the economic conditions that affect the lives of our people.
I submit that a great deal more is at stake than just the cost of living, important as that is at the present time. Involved in this whole question is the future of democracy itself. Democracy cannot go backward; it cannot stand still. It must move forward. Democracy involves freedom and the control by the people of the country, through their elected representatives, of the things that affect them all. If we are to maintain our political freedom and civil liberties we must move on to economic freedom and economic democracy, and if the house passes this motion it will be taking a step in that very necessary direction.

Mr. Speaker, if I did not rise to express my views on this measure I should feel that I were remiss in my duty and negligent of the welfare of the constituents whom I have the honour to represent.
During the years of the war the government took to itself pride and credit for the initiation of a policy, of subsidies and price control, and speeches which have been made in this house quite recently indicate quite clearly that, as a result of this policy, great savings have accrued to the Canadian people. When -we compare the results of price control in Canada and the United States we feel that we have great cause for pride, and I for one like to give credit where credit is due, whether it be to this government or to any other. If price control has been good for the Canadian people-and again I say that it has been shown that controls have been good-then why this unseemly haste to abolish them? I know, as every member of the house knows, that great pressure has been brought to bear on the government to remove price controls, but I am very sure that that pressure has not come from the housewives and the families of Canada. They are viewing with alarm the threat to their well-being which is contained in the rising cost of living. Personally I cannot understand the attitude of the government in thus yielding weakly to the pressure of big business to remove controls in the face of the rising resentment on the part of the electorate. It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that the time is fast approaching when the government should have its ear to the ground so as to know and understand the temper and attitude of the people preparatory to a general election, but on the contrary the government seems to be riding high and very handsome disregarding

entirely the resentment and the expressed wishes of the people. The people today expect of a government that held prices steady during the war that it will hold prices steady during this recurring time of peace.
During the war I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking over the radio, make a statement to this effect, that the people of Canada now' have more money than they ever had before, presumably because of the high wages received from war work. Personally I think the Prime Minister's statement was unw'ise, because there were at that time many thousands of Canadian people whose wages had not been increased because of war work and who certainly had no more money in their pockets at that time than they had before. Necessary spending in many families was restricted during the war time by compulsory savings and, by the way, the people today are very anxious to connect again with those compulsory savings which wrere withheld from them.
But my deepest concern todaj' is for the people in the low' income brackets, the men and the women who are feeling very keenly indeed the rising cost of living-the old age pensioners, our sick and infirm people, our unemployed, for we do have them. It may interest hon. members to know that the provincial government of British Columbia has dismissed, in the city of Fernie, w'hich I represent, all its employees over the age of sixty-five. No provision whatsoever is being made for the way in which these people shall live. They are not eligible at the present time for the old age pension, and they are finding that the cost of living is soaring day by day and hurting them considerably. I wonder if this government expects that these dismissed employees will vote at a coming election for the Liberal party, for a party that has failed to hold prices at a time when they need to be held very strictly indeed.

Consequently the farmer is squeezed, as I have said, between two pressures. The economy tells him what others will pay him for the goods he has to sell, while it tells him at the same time what prices he will have to pay for the things he has to buy. The result is that he is soon squeezed out. There will have to be some control if we are to prevent complete chaos.
The farmer saw that in the days prior to the war. Now he sees prices set on farm commodities. He has accepted a set price for farm commodities. He believes it is a good thing. I think the majority of the farmers of the country have supported the wheat agreement with the United Kingdom, because it gives a guarantee of an initial price of $1.35 for a period of years. The farmer has forgone the present world price. He says that is better than the fluctuations we have had. At any rate he knows he is going to get that, and that has been set. But, may I point out, all the advantages that may accrue from that, can be wiped out overnight if there is no control over the prices of the commodities he has to buy. If you turn the implement companies and the monopolies loose and let them put up prices as they wish; if you take the ceilings off gasoline, distillates, binder twine, clothing, sugar, the things he has to buy, then this set price that he has agreed to will mean absolutely nothing to him.

He said:	Mr. Speaker, at this stage on

The 1941 census gave the population as 817,861. According to the ration books issued-and this was only a short time ago-the population of British Columbia is now 1,019,745.
