Application of B.C. Telephone Company to increase its capital stock
Dear Sir:
I wish to notify you of the following recommendation of the harbours, utilities and airport committee, dated February 10, 1947, which was adopted by council on February 17, 1947:
"Recommended that the following report, dated February 3, 1947. from the special committee comprising the chairman (Aid. Thompson), Aldermen Miller and Gervin and the corporation counsel, with regard to the subject matter, be approved and the company be so notified:
The application of this company to increase its capital stock from $11,000,000 to $25,000,000 and to effect the repeal of subsection (3) of section 6 of its Incorporation Act, was referred by council on the 27th ultimo to the undersigned as a special committee with instructions to report to your committee at its next meeting.
We have had an interview with Mr. Gordon Farrell, president, Mr. C. B. Diplock, general manager, and Brigadier Sherwood Lett, counsel for the company.
We are impressed with the fact that the company requires fresh capital in substantial amounts to meet the backlog of deferred instalments during the war as well as the normal expansion of its business. Under its charter the company even if authority of parliament is given to increase its capitalization, cannot make any issue, sale or other disposition of the new capital without first obtaining the approval of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. No question of rates is directly involved in such increased capitalization because rates are specifically under the control of the board of transport commissioners and the company agrees to give to the city notice of any application for a change in rates that might affect its subscribers in Vancouver.
We have also considered the company's application to repeal subsection (3) of section 6 added to the company's charter in 1941. Having regard to modern principles of rate making, we think the section is of little importance either to the city or to the company. As, however, it was apparently added to the act with the intention of serving as a measure of protection to the company's subscribers, we make no recommendation on the application with respect to it.
Our recommendation is that the company be notified that the city has no objection to the amendment by which it seeks to increase its authorized capital from $11,000,000 to $25,000,000, subject always to the approval of the
Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to the issue, sale or other disposition of such stock or any part thereof."
I think that is all I need say at this time. I am asking the house to be good enough to give this bill second reading and let it go to the committee on railways and canals.

speechtext:
Mr. WILFRID LaCROIX (Quebec-Mont-morency) moved the second reading of Bill No. 133, to amend the Criminal Code (illegal organizations).
He said: The bill I am submitting this evening for the approval of this house, the object of which is the suppression of any

Criminal Code Amendment
kind of communistic party in Canada, is selfexplanatory and should not require very much debate in order to justify it. As all hon. members know, Mr. Igor Gouzenko recently exposed the Soviet spy rings in Canada. To the following question, "What attitude should Canada adopt towards the Canadian communist party?" Mr. Gouzenko replied:
The communist party in Canada is not just a political party like other major political parties in this country. It is an agency of the Soviet Union, which aims to overthrow our system of government. Canadians must never lose sight of that fact.
The free existence of the communist party here astounds, more than anything else, every soviet person who arrives in a democratic country from the Soviet Union. They know perfectly well whose interests that party is serving. Taught from their experience in the Soviet Union, where the democratic elements were mercilessly destroyed long ago, and where only the communist party has the right to exist, these soviet people expect to see the same picture in the democratic countries. They expect to see the communist party banned, and the leaders of that party in jails, or liquidated.
Their surprise is, therefore, equally great when they see that the communist party functions openly and propagates anti-democratic ideas, the while it takes advantage of a constitution which ensures its right to print and issue its newspapers, to broadcast on the radio, to hold meetings, and all this with the aim of overthrowing the same constitution which gives it this right.
Allow me to say, Mr. Speaker, that I was bewildered to find that in one constituency alone, six thousand Canadians have, during a recent by-election, clearly shown their adherence to the communist party. According to Mr. Gouzenko, the most important factor of the communistic programme is absolute allegiance to Moscow.
I would request that hon. members adopt the second reading of the bill, since it involves its principle. This bill has been in the hands of members of the house since before the Easter recess, and they should by now have found the time to read it in its entirety. Should hon. members wish to suggest amendments, they will be afforded the opportunity to do so in committee when the sections of the bill will be examined in detail.
For instance, section 1 stipulates the following:
The communist party of Canada, the Labour Progressive party of Canada and any association, society, group or organization having similar aims or purposes are declared to be, and shall be deemed to be illegal organizations:	Provided
that no association, society, group or organization, except the communist party of Canada, and the Labour Progressive party shall be deemed to be an illegal organization unless the governor in council has, by notice published in
the Canada Gazette declared the said association, society, group or organization to be an illegal association within the meaning of this section.
The reason behind this wording is that no one is in a better position than the government, with the assistance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to have the necessary information which would allow it to make a decision in the matter.
However, should certain members of the house ascribe to this section powers which are too arbitrary to be placed in the hands of a government, nothing should prevent an amendment from being tabled in committee, which would force the government to submit this information, documentation and evidence to the Supreme Court of Canada, which would decide without appeal.
Since no amendment may be made on second reading, it is vital that the principle itself be decided upon by allowing the bill to be passed on second reading. I therefore count on the good will of the members of this house in this matter.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley for the second reading of Bill No. 104, to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles.

speechtext:
I should like to give a ruling on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), which reads as follows:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the headlong decontrol policy of the government has depressed the standard of living
Emergency Powers

of the people, threatens the country with economic chaos, and is surrendering the future of Canada to profiteering and monopoly;
And be it further resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to the introduction of a system of orderly and democratic controls and the restoration of lower prices for the necessities of life, particularly articles of food and clothing, soap and shortening, shelter, household appliances, and supplies and machinery needed in agriculture, in order to eliminate the injustices which now exist and to arrest the rapidly rising cost of living.
I wish to call the attention of the hon. member to citation 357 at page 139 of Beau-chesne, third edition, which reads as follows: Mr. Speaker Sproule on the 13th February, 1913, decided that a proposed amendment which was substantially the same motion as the member had moved on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, was not in order because "a motion must not raise a question substantially identical with one on which the house has given a decision in the same session."
I would also direct attention to the ruling given by the Hon. George Black, Speaker, on March 14, 1934, which is found at page 714 of the same edition, in these words:
A motion dealing with a question moved and rejected as an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne is out of order.
The hon. member will recall that on March 7. during this session, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) moved the following amendment:
We respectfully submit, however, that in the opinion of this house Your Excellency's advisers have shown a readiness to return to the policies of uncontrolled and unplanned private enterprise which resulted in the depression and unemployment in prewar years . . .
The first part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre being substantially the same as the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I have no hesitation in saying that the amendment is out of order. As far as the second part of the amendment moved by the hon. member is concerned, I would call his attention to May, 13th edition, page . 391, where he will find the following:
Nor may such an amendment deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee . . .
I therefore rule the amendment out of order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to hear your ruling with regard to this amendment, but we are going to abide by your decision without challenging it at this time.
Before the dinner recess, in dealing with the principle of this bill I was discussing the 
various effects of price control and trying to point out to the house that the time has come when in an economy such as we have in Canada it is essential to protect the people against the ravages of monopolistic enterprises and to have some democratic control that will say to these people, "This is a fair price, this is a just price, this is the price to which you are entitled and over and above that there is not to be exploitation; we intend to stop it."
I was pointing out that by the removal of controls over prices by a government body we are not thereby removing controls. The controls are still there. Prices will then be dictated by the people who control the commodities. One monopolistic organization or another has the supplies completely within its hands and it says to those who come to buy them, "You pay this price or you go without." It seems to me that in days such as these, with industry organized as it is in this country today, this country or any other country similarly organized cannot be without some measure of price control to protect its people.
I ask the house to consider the position of the working man, the position of the farmer and the position of the pensioner who are squeezed between the cost of living and the wages that they earn. The farmer is squeezed between the cost of the things he must buy in order to produce and the prices; which he receives for the commodities he sells. He finds that the prices of these-things are dictated to him. We have little right to say that there is no dictatorship in Canada. Prices are dictated to him when he goes to buy the commodities he needs and when he goes to sell his products he is told the price he will get.
I think we are coming to the dividing of the ways. Are we to remove all control by the government and let private and monopolistic enterprise go unbridled, allow prices to. go higher and higher with no redress, no board, to appeal to, with reduced production, lower living standards, unemployment; back again to the old routine that we have gone through for the past forty years, depression, war, a period of prosperity, depression again and. then war coming on as the only release? We have a continuous procession in which the common man finds himself hopeless and helpless to fight against the tide of those who control.
The common man, the farmer in particular, finds that in order to fight he must organize himself into groups. The cooperative movement is nothing more or less than a sign of

Emergency Powers
the times on the part of the common people, an effort to protect themselves against the ravages of monopolistic enterprises. They must have some control over the commodities which they are selling in order that they may have some say as to the prices at which those commodities shall be sold. The organization of a trade union is nothing more than a group of people getting together to say, "The wages we are receiving are too low in order to pay rising costs of living; we have nothing to sell but the sweat of our brow, and therefore we must have some say as to what we are going to sell our commodity for."
I noticed that as soon as the government released these controls it turned around and pleaded with big business to be careful and to be sensible. I would point out the fact that a similar appeal was made by the President of the United States and I would refer hon. members to what happened in the United States after the removal last year of controls under the OPA. The financial editor of the Globe and Mail on April 12 lists the United States weekly commodity prices. Taking 1926 as 100, he shows that in August, 1939, the index was 63-7; in March, 1946, it was 114-7; on January 3 of this year, 150-2; on March of this year, 166. Those are the index levels as compared with 1926. What is to be the outcome? How far is this to continue? The President is certainly disappointed in the effects of the removal of price controls.
If there is no check on the operations of competition evening things up, but where is these enterprises, what will they do? They will have complete control. We talk about your competition? Monopolistic enterprise does not recognize competition. What it says is this: "We will cut the throat of any small competitor, but we will cooperate with the big boys who compete in the same field." If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) wants to start taxing cooperators he should start at the top and tax those who are really cooperating in the way of fixing prices.
We all know the hue and cry that is raised as soon as anybody says anything about controlling the prices which big business wants to charge. Many people seem to consider organizations such as International Nickel as being the real essence of democracy; but as soon as any cooperative enterprise, like our great wheat pools in western Canada, get started they are charged with being communistic and socialistic. Some people seem to think that is communism. They consider the operations of a monopoly to exploit the people as they wish as being real democracy. As soon as any one challenges their right to
exploit the people there is the cry that we are establishing a dictatorship; that this is socialism. They are ready to tie it up with communism, Russian spies and espionage. They want to start a holy crusade to save our families and homes.
When the common man organizes into a cooperative organization in an endeavour to fight against the forces which he finds are turned loose in this land and when such an organization endorses the maintenance of price control it is contended that they are setting up a dictatorship. What we are fighting is a form of dictatorship which is abroad in this country and which at times makes it impossible for a man to make a living. It is impossible for the common people to establish the kind of homes they should have if we are to make this Canada of ours a great country.
The whole set-up has failed, and failed dismally. Actually the control exercised by monopoly in this country is one of the worst forms of exploitation I can think of. Jesse James was a piker compared with these fellows. He went out with a gun and a blind over his eyes to rob people, but today it is legalized. These fellows go around with the law on their side and with lawyers and the sheriff to protect them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit a question, would he prefer to live in this awful country of Canada or in either of the two countries where controls existed prior to the war, in Italy or Germany?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Of course I would prefer to live in a country where there is democracy and democratic control. I would not want to live under any kind of dictatorship. Here, Mr. Speaker, is a repetition of the cry to which I was referring a few moments ago. But I say that Canada is not yet half the country she might be. Here we are located on the northern half of the North American continent, a country of great natural resources but with only 12,000,000 people where we might well have 20.000,000. Our population drifted across the United States border, and a million of our people were on relief. We are heading into unemployment again. It is to prevent just such a thing that, we require controls. Those controls have to be exercised by a democratic government. In a resolution which the Progressive Conservative party introduced on April 1 they declared they were unalterably opposed to the enactment of any measure w-hich would give sweeping powers to boards outside the control of parliament. Of course we would not want pow-ers to be given to boards that are outside the control of
Emergency Powers

parliament. The government in operating the wartime prices and trade board operates it under a department of this government. The board exercises control over prices and the minister is responsible to parliament for the actions of the board. He can be questioned in the house and called upon by the democratic representatives duly elected by the Canadian people to answer for the policies which the board is carrying out. That is responsible, democratic control. No one believes that we should give powers to boards that are not answerable to anyone. Large corporations have to answer to no one today, but parliament can and does exercise democratic control over boards set up by parliament. Such parliamentary control is the essence of democracy. To assume that because you support a board that is under democratic control by parliament you are in favour of establishing a dictatorship is utter nonsense.
The Canadian people require a shield to protect the masses of our people against the ravages of unbridled private enterprise. It is because of the failure of the system that controls have become necessary. I believe it is an established fact that the development of industry in the direction it has taken necessitates this very thing, and I doubt that any government could continue long in Canada without such controls. When you relax these controls and give free rein to private enterprise you are quickening the downward march of the Canadian people into unemployment, to lower standards of living, higher costs, lack of production, lack of ability to maintain a proper income level to enable the Canadian people to meet the costs of government and the costs of the war. The costs of the war to the Canadian people have not yet been met. The national debt of this country has mounted to over $15 billion, which means that we must maintain a high income level for the masses of the Canadian people, not just those at the top, but the great masses of our people. It means that we must. establish an economy under which the masses of our people may have decent homes where they will be free from fear and free from want.
Surveys made recently show that in Canada, the United States, Great Britain and even Sweden the population is not being maintained because people will not raise children to live in poverty and in want. Fathers and mothers will not be responsible for bringing children into a world where they will suffer from want, poverty, hunger, and the fear of war. In Canada we are not maintaining our natural increase in population. Already there are signs of a declining birthrate. To counteract that, we must see that conditions are

established where people will not live within the shadow of unemployment but will have some measure of security and a decent standard of living.
We are deciding today what Canada of the future shall be, and I take a chance on prophesying that if controls are completely lifted Canada will be headed into another period of unemployment. Already there are signs of it in the eastern maritime provinces. We find higher costs and a lower standard of living, unemployment, and a demand from the people for redress and that parliament shall exercise some measure of control to protect them from the ravages of monopolistic enterprise. It is those who sit in responsible positions on the benches in this house who will be held responsible by the people if these controls are let go, and the people will repudiate those who say of private enterprise: Leave it free to go all the way and the situation will correct itself. For the sake of the Canada of the future, and of the near future, I plead with the members of this house to think seriously of the consequences of removing controls completely. Think of what kind of Canada we would have under those circumstances! The question before us is more than simply a matter of political necessity at the present time, of giving what people here and there may be clamouring for or what the press may be demanding. The press is finding that it has made its mistakes. Let us learn from the mistakes that have been made by our great neighbour to the south and lay the foundations now for a Canada which can be truly great.

Dealing with the observations of the hon. member for Yorkton, who has just interrupted me, may I point out to him the situation with regard to farmers, who, he complains, are not enabled to enjoy a proper standard of living. I point out that the farmers are getting prices today which are higher than they received at any other time during the hon. member's lifetime. They are enjoying higher prices for their products than at any other time in the history of Canada.
The hon. member says that those doing business with private enterprise have no redress. Why, the consumer holds the controlling hand in any market. That is recognized both in this country and in the United States. If the merchant, the manufacturer or the wholesaler runs wild the consumer can bring him back to a proper sense of values because of that buying control which the consumer exercises, and because of that control we shall not have the sky-rocketing of prices in Canada which was experienced in the United States for a short time.
With regard to the principle of controls and decontrols, if there is one country in the world whose government should be complimented on the policy it is carrying out in this regard it is Canada, and that government is the government which is in power here. I might differ with my hon. friends of the Conservative party who advocate complete decontrol and I say that it is not a proper time for a complete decontrol policy. I advocate, and right along have stated that controls during war time are absolutely necessary. Further, I do not hesitate to say that controls should continue until Canada has gone through the transition period and properly rearranged production so as to supply the market in a reasonable and safe manner. That, I think, is the policy that has been pursued up to the present time.
Whether the government will in the future decontrol too quickly remains to be seen, but I would point out that this bill is for the purpose of providing proper controls. If we find that the manufacturers are allowing things to get out of hand the government can recontrol certain items of luxuries or other commodities as they see fit There is a reason why Canada should look forward to great expansion, and as a free enterpriser I believe that expansion must be carried on, not alone by the twenty-six firms cited by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I am thinking of the thousands of small manufacturing concerns throughout the country who throw into their efforts the very best they have. I am thinking of the large number of individual owners who have a small number of employees, not of the twenty-six large firms which are so often referred to by the leader of the C.C.F. and members of that group.
My hon. friends, it seems to me, wish to draw a red herring over the trail in regard to the fine effort being made by the great majority of the smaller manufacturers, and for that reason I do not think they are fair in their criticisms. As I have said on more than one occasion, I always enjoy listening to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Perhaps some of my hon. friends on this side, the Liberal side, will say, "Why pay so many compliments to the leader of the CCF and build him up?" Well, I like to be honest. At the same time I warn the hon. gentleman that he is doing Canada a discredit by allow-
Emergency Powers

ing his followers to go from one end of the country to the other creating fear by reminding people of the period from 1930 to 1935.
I do not refer to this period for any political purpose but because I do not think we want to see a return of those conditions. We do not want a depression, and I do not think we shall see a return of those conditions if we follow the policy laid down by this government, which provided such wonderful leadership during the war, and which has made such plans for the post-war period as will bring industry back to a safe and sane way of producing the necessities to supply the need that exists so definitely today.
There is scarcity; we all know that. How will you overcome that scarcity? You can overcome it only by production, and production means employment. My hon. friend has referred to people like myself as Jesse Jameses. Why, Jesse James was a piker alongside the member who has the floor at the present time, he would lead you to believe. Jesse James was a piker alongside those fellows. What fellows does he refer to? The fellows who in the war tried, and in the future will still try, to build a better, brighter and more prosperous Canada. Those are the fellows referred to as Jesse Jameses.
The hon. member refers to certain types of businessmen as cutting the throat of the small fellow. That sounds good from a public platform in' certain districts but not on the floor of the house when it is sent broadcast throughout the country. I am not trying to lecture the hon. member; I would not dare to do so; but why should we have a constant repetition of this hackneyed phrase about the common man? I am just a common man myself, and so are we all. I do not think that does a bit of good. The common people are the people I depend upon for a living in my business. It is not being up here. It is my business that gives me a living, and I am going to look after that business. How am I going to look after it? By doing what I consider to be fair to the men who are dealing with me. I think the remarks of the hon. member about ravishes of private enterprise are very much uncalled for.
I think Canada is a wonderful country. No other one has greater supplies of basic materials. Our natural resources fall into five main classes:	farm, lands, mineral areas,
forests, waterpower and fisheries. These contribute in varying degrees to the whole national income. Not only or even mainly by the sale of raw materials but by the use of the products shall we be successful in building a bigger Canada with a greater opportunity for export

business and domestic business. I believe if the people of Canada understood this bill and the purpose of it, which is to control in such a way as to carry on for the period named in the bill until such a time as we resume along natural lines and are able to produce and supply those articles that are scarce at the present time, they would appreciate it; I believe that the sooner the people realize the purposes of this bill, the sooner they will know what a fine job this government is doing in bringing into effect a bill of this type.
I had no thought, Mr. Speaker, of speaking at any length; but, since I am a firm believer that the progress and future development of this country rest to a very large extent on the men known as free enterprisers, I could not sit here and allow such remarks as have been made to go unchallenged. I should like to have dealt with some of the points raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) this afternoon. In the main I agree with him, but I question the wisdom-and I am sincere in this-of decontrolling at too rapid a pace. I wish to throw out a suggestion to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) and others who have studied this matter of controls and decontrols. I compliment them upon their policy up to the present time and suggest, because of the effect that it might have on the so-called organized labour forces of this country that if decontrol comes too quickly it might possibly force them to continue to make requests to industry for higher wages and thus slow up what we hope will be continued progress in regard to production.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I spoke a little too warmly on this subject. Free enterprise is, of course, to me a subject to which I am very close. I began life on my own hook, so to speak, and I have competed with these big fellows, these so-called giants that some people think are after the little fellow all the time.
I never had very much unfair criticism; in fact, I would criticize the so-called big fellow as quickly as the C.C.F. criticize all the rest of Canada who do not fall in line with them. But on the whole I think the big fellow wants to do what is right. He has his own ideas as to what will be best for Canada. I feel that we are all working in the same way to bring about better times or continuing good times for Canada.
In connection with the decontrols which have already gone into effect, it is only fair that I should point out that a very large number of the retail stores have already advertised through the press and made it known that they did not propose to increase in price

Emergency Powers
any stock which they have on hand. There are always exceptions to the rule. Yesterday someone cited-I think it was the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar-the example of chocolate bars, that chocolate bars had been raised from six to eight cents. It is unfortunate that the manufacturers of that particular article saw fit to do that. That is one case. They raised the price of their chocolates. Of course that is the same industry. But when you think of the very large number of wholesalers and retailers who have publicly announced that there will be no change in regard to their price lists, then I say they far outweigh the few who have adopted the other course.
In closing, I just wish to repeat what I have said on more than one occasion, that I believe free enterprise is doing a good job for Canada and that without this unfair criticism it will continue to do a good job and bring Canada back to a normal state and will continue the prosperity we have enjoyed and the high standard of living we have had in this fine country.

It seems that we might be welcome with a contribution to this debate. We believe that the members on the various sides of the house have pretty well talked themselves into a state of mind in which they realize that something must be done different from what has been advocated by any of the three, shall we say, major parties in this house. All hon. members I think have indicated a good sense of the problem facing us. I was particularly pleased with the speech made by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) this afternoon. A good many others have given fine speeches, showing the difficulties before the house, but not realizing to any great extent what can be done about the difficulty. May I make a brief contribution on the subject?
Before going forward, I should like to refer to the speech made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) this afternoon. I think he gave a rather brilliant and witty speech, although he was considerably under par this afternoon because, instead of clarifying the situation, he added confusion. If there is any one thing that the members of this house ought to do when they rise to speak- if hon. members will pardon me for making the suggestion-it is this:	Let us clarify the
issue. Let us not confuse it. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) so well said this afternoon in an excellent speech, I thought, every man in this
house is trying to find out how to solve the difficulties; and, make no mistake about it, every member of this house and every group in this house has a distinct contribution to make, and no group in this house can afford to treat slightingly the contribution of any other group. To make remarks such as the hon. member for Cape Breton South made to the effect that social crediters do not believe in anything except just printing a lot of money, is simply to show either profound misinformation concerning the matter or a levity which is hardly to be excused.

We will grant that, but we must allow people time to mature. You cannot expect people to come full-fledged into this house and speak freely without making little blunders occasionally. They will get their feet on the ground after a while, and you will not find any confusion at all. Recently we have had a number of people speaking from among our party who have not spoken to any great extent during the ten or eleven years we have been here; but there have been certain members of this group who have spoken for the group, and those people have never wavered or deviated one jot or tittle since the first day they came into this house. They have preached a straightforward doctrine, logical and consistent all the time, and are still preaching it.
That having been said, may I now turn to some other matters? As I have just said, the Social Credit group has always spoken consistently in favour of certain principles. The first of those is that they have favoured inducement controls. When we first came into the house a number of hon. members were alarmed. They said that we believed in regimentation, that we would simply build up a dictatorship, and all that sort of thing. The only kind of thing we were advocating was controls by inducement. That goes right to
Emergency Powers

the heart of the problem today. What we need in this country is controls by inducement. In the discussion recently a number of our C.C.F. friends have shown that they desire controls by inducement. They talk about desiring freedom, and of their wish to increase their freedom. They will increase their freedom by introducing controls by inducement rather than controls by regulation or coercion. I shall say a few words about that later on, but I wish to emphasize that particular point because it goes right to the heart of the problem confronting Canada and the world today: controls by inducement rather than controls by coercion. Just as soon as you begin to pass laws demanding that people do such and such, fixing prices, fixing wages and so on, then you begin to build up dictatorial concepts which are likely to result in a totalitarian state. On the other hand, if you can bring in measures which will induce people to do the right thing, then you are on the way to a greater measure of democracy and freedom. The social credit movement has consistently advocated controls by inducement right from the very beginning. As the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) well said, and I should like to give him credit for it, ever since he has known the social crediters they have spoken of fair prices. That is quite right. It is impossible to have fair prices without inducement controls; and the mere fact that social credit advocates have consistently spoken in favour of fair prices and just prices has implied as clearly as possibly could be implied that they favour inducement controls. And we still favour inducement controls. I would challenge any member of the C.C.F. group or any other member of the house to point to a single occasion, in Hansard or anywhere else, when responsible members of this group, speaking for the group, have said anything to the contrary.

speechtext:
Oh, I know vou
can say a lot of smart things. I can say them too, if I have to. I challenge any member of the C.C.F. or any other party to show where responsible members of this group, speaking for the group throughout the years, have advocated anything but controls by inducement to bring about fair prices, fair wages and a regular, ordered economy.
The Social Credit group has always favoured private enterprise, responsible private enter-

prise. There have been members who have tried to convey-and the hon. member for Cape Breton South was one of them this time-the idea that social crediters are in favour of unlimited free enterprise, that they agree with the Conservatives and Liberals in this respect. No one who knows anything about social credit will make that blunder, unless he just wants to play politics. We have always, as a group, favoured private enterprise because we believe, when business is conducted by private people who are concerned about the success of their own business, they will produce more efficiently both as to quantity and as to quality than will government-owned enterprise. We point to the simple fact that the free enterprise of the private enterprise nations has simply overwhelmed and swamped the nations that depended on government ownership whenever they have come into conflict with those nations. The last war was the finest possible illustration of that, when the United States utterly overwhelmed all opposition with the production from private enterprise, and Canada did simply marvellously in production, because she was following the private enterprise system.
No one can say that private enterprise has failed. As I pointed out in my speech in this house on March 7, why be foolish enough to say private enterprise has failed in the light of the marvellous achievements which can be chalked up to the credit of private enterprise? It is not private enterprise that has failed. We do not need to change from private enterprise to public enterprise. What we need to do is introduce some device whereby we can allow private enterprise to produce to the fullest desirable degree under the circumstances, and then enable the people to purchase and consume the goods private enterprise is able to produce, thereby raising the standard of living, the standard of employment, the standard of prosperity and everything else that is good in the nation. That is the thing we want.
Let us see the line we must follow in order to find that thing we wish to secure. I believe I have made it quite clear that social credit is not in favour of free enterprise that results iD monopolies or cartels. It is in favour of private enterprise regulated in such a way as to avoid the abuses and monstrosities which result from unrestricted, unregulated free enterprise. Now may I submit to the house in all seriousness that the time has come right now for the members of the government and the members of this house to consider with the most earnest care the introduction of social credit. This means that the time has come to change the

Emergency Powers
Canadian financial system in one or two important respects, to enable that system to distribute goods as it now so magnificently produces goods. The cost of living simply must not be permitted to rise; I think every hon. member has advocated this idea. There is not a member anywhere in this house who wants to see the cost of living continue to rise. The trouble is the}' do not know how to stop it. What can we do about finding out how to stop it? Prices simply must be controlled. Just prices for both primary and secondary producers and for consumers must be maintained. That is a problem the solution of which requires much care and much skill. Just wages must be maintained. I was quite well pleased with the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Cape Breton South this afternoon with respect to the Nova Scotia coal workers. Those workers in Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces absolutely must receive the means of a higher standard of living. If they do not this nation is going to rue the day. As long as those people are kept in poverty or semi-poverty, that fact stands as a disgrace to every person in public life in this dominion; and the nearer he is to the Prime Minister of this country, the greater the disgrace. The problem simply must be solved, and it must not be solved by being turned over blithely to the provincial administration. It is a coward's trick to turn the problem over to provincial administration: after we have allowed it to grow to such dimensions that even the dominion is unable to deal with it, then to have the dominion government go down and hide behind the skirts of the provinces! Yet we have to listen to that sort of thing from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and from other people in the house from time to time.
Now that problem must be solved How? That is the question. It can be solved. Two methods of control have been employed by the government in power during this war. I am astonished that they have not learned the lesson which was so obviously taught during the -war. First of all, they used the method of coercion, or prohibition by law. If any person sold an article above the celing price, and the offence was discovered, that person paid a penalty, and it was a pretty severe one. That was the law. It was control by law, or coercion. It worked fairly well during the war, while the people were under the stress of many different kinds of emotions. But it does not work very well in peace time. It is not the device which is desirable, because it leads to totalitarianism.
The other method the government used was that of control by inducement-by subsidy, or bonus. I do not suppose any government in the British commonwealth, or perhaps in the whole world, went farther than our government did in the matter of subsidizing prices in one way or another, by direct and indirect means, so as to keep prices down. Hon. members will recall how the price of oranges was kept down and how the price of milk was kept down, and the prices of a great many other commodities.
At this point I wish to commend the then Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), who was in charge during those years, for the superb success which attended his efforts. The important thing I would suggest, is that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who has succeeded the Minister of Justice, shall go forward with that device in peace time, and that he shall not imagine that the principle of subsidies is unsound. The principle of subsidies was a completely sound principle. It was used in Great Britain, the United States and Canada, with signal success. Then why should anyone suppose that it is not a sound principle? It is a principle of control by inducement.
I have mentioned the two methods of control which have been used with success in this country, and which we can examine at the present time as possibilities for greater use in the future. Social crediters favour the deep and broad application of the principle of control of prices, through subsidies, the control of wages through bonuses, it having been agreed upon, after careful study by representatives of all groups concerned just what ought to be accepted as a fair price for any given commodity, allowing for a fair profit and just what ought to be accepted as a fair wage for any given service.
To illustrate:	Let us keep in mind, so far
as wages are concerned, the wage scale schedule which prevailed, say, in the railroad systems. Wage rates have been determined by careful study and agreement. The various relations of all people who are working throughout the whole system are all set down and agreed upon as being fair. That sort of thing should prevail throughout the whole nation, in respect of the wages of the nation; and once that has been agreed upon, then the next problem is to take steps to see that the financial support which is necessary is provided to maintain that wage structure.
A similar thing can be done with respect to prices. We have already gone a long way in determining what ought to be the price of wheat, for example, and various other commodities. To my mind, it is not beyond the
Emergency Powers

ability of the brilliant minds which are so numerous in Canada to get together and to agree on what ought to be the fair prices for wheat, oats, barley, meat, eggs and all those various other things we produce in a primary way, for all the various commodities we produce in a secondary way such as shoes, hats, furniture and all those other things we produce. We ought to be able to determine what is a fair price. Having determined that price, let us find the financial means of supporting that price, and maintaining it throughout the country .
Such having been done, such agreement having been attained, and the price structure and wage structure ascertained, it ought to be supported, sustained and maintained by means of subsidies and bonuses. Under such circumstances there would be no fixing of prices, no fixing of wages by any arbitrary body. This is where I believe the tendency of social crediters is to go off at a tangent from the C.C.F. Whether our good C.C.F. friends really mean to set up an arbitrary body which will fix prices and wages, I am not sure. But a great many of the things they say lead me to believe that they envisage having the representatives of the various elements concerned in the production of a commodity meeting together to agree on the price and the wage. That is a perfectly democratic way of doing it. It is a process of arriving at a price and agreeing on a wage without fixing it by an arbitrary body.
Social crediters are opposed to the idea of fixing. They are all in favour of the idea of agreeing or arriving at it by compromise and study. There are people who have gone off at a tangent, I think, in respect of social credit. I am speaking particularly for social crediters across the country, and for those who wish to know what the great social credit authorities favour. In this connection I should like to quote some passages from great social credit authorities. I shall quote so as to show that what I have said here tonight is perfectly sound in respect of the social credit attitude with respect to controls.
I turn first of all to "Social Credit" by Major C. H. Douglas, published in 1937 in revised form, and I quote from the appendix at page 208, which deals with a draft social credit scheme for Scotland. It states: Simultaneously with the publication of the foregoing notice-
And the foregoing notice refers to the dividend which, although we are not saying very much about it, is still a very living thing.

-a figure to be published known as the discount rate to replace the existing hank discount rate, a suitable value of this for initial purposes being 25 per cent.
That amounts, I might say, for those who wish to know, to a subsidy. It brings down the price of the goods. Then he continues:
It is important that the figure should not be less than 25 per cent, and it might reasonably be higher.
Simultaneously, an announcement to be published that any or all business undertakings will be accepted for registration under an assisted price scheme.
I interpolate to point out that they are not going to be registered. They are not going to be listed. They will be accepted for registration upon their own volition. I proceed to read:
The conditions of such registration will be that their accounts, as at present required under the Companies Acts, should contain an additional item showing the average profit on turnover, and that their prices shall, as far as practicable, be maintained at a figure to include such average profit, where this is agreed as equitable for the type of business concerned (the suitable profit being of course, largely dependent on the velocity of turnover).
I pause to comment there that it will be noted by those who have followed these words that social credit is not opposed to profit. It favours the profit motive as being perhaps the finest incentive ever discovered by man to encourage people to produce. But it does not agree with allowing the profit to be determined at will, or through the whims of the people who are making the profits. This profit is agreed upon, after study, as being the proper profit, having in mind the possible turnover; and having been agreed upon, it is held to by all concerned.
May I quote from one other authority, this time from the "A.B.C. of Social Credit" by E. S. Holter, published in 1944. Before 1 commence reading, may I point out that this book is accepted by Major Douglas as being authentic. He has said of it that it is a straightforward, honest and simple outline of social credit; and of course members in this group accept it. There has been no deviation by members of this group from the ideas and opinions, both economic and financial, of the great founder of the movement, Major C. H. Douglas. I read from page 49 as follows:
To put the foregoing proposal into effect would not imply the elimination of competition in industry-there would be no fixing of prices. Taking a fair price level as a basis (not a level conditioned by a period of either inflation or deflation) prices would vary as today according to the variety of commodity being sold. The retailer availing himself of the discount would obviously be able to undersell those who preferred not to make use of it.

Emergency Powers
May I interpolate there for the sake of those who are following so closely. It is quite obvious that there is no desire to force people to use the discount. We will say a large company selling coal is able, by coming under the scheme, to sell its coal twenty-five per cent lower than it could under ordinary circumstances. If the company does not choose to come under the scheme and accept that privilege of selling under the discount, that is entirely a matter for the company to decide. But that company will soon find itself in competition with other companies which are selling under the discount and will feel the pinch and be induced to fall in line. Our C.C.F. friends and a good many others throughout the house are quite disturbed over monopolies, but they will find no monopoly in the country which cannot be brought under control by inducement. I proceed to quote:
The question of profits might conceivably ruin all the benefits to be derived from the application of the "just price." What is to prevent producers from raising their prices sky high and then using the discount purely to their own advantage? The answer is simply this-that producers wishing to avail themselves of the right to dispense the discount would have to agree to a fair but fixed profit on turnover. To put it another way, using a hypothetical illustration-a producer will be offered a proposition such as the following: "If you will agree to continue to sell an article at $20 instead of raising the price to $25, by being eligible to dispense the discount you can offer that article to the consumer for $15, the sum of $5 being reimbursed to you through the national credit account." Now- though in some instances profits on individual sales v-ould be less than they are today, the fact that the producer is enabled to sell his articles below cost, assures him of a far greater number of sales. In this -way his increased turnover would more than compensate for any decrease of profit on individual sales. If he rejects this offer and sells a portion of his goods at whatever price they will fetch, he runs the risk of having a large portion of his goods remaining for they will be in competition with goods benefiting by the discount. Here it must be observed that there is no compulsion involved. The producer makes his own choice.
Just a -word or two further and I will close this technical discussion, technical because technicalities are necessary because of the difficulties which confront us. The question will arise, "Where is the money coming from?" This is the question the Liberals will be asking constantly. The Minister of Finance will be asking constantly, "Where is the money to come from?" Let me say once more, even at the risk of having people, as did the hon. member for Cape Breton South this afternoon, superficially sneer at the idea, that the money can be created under certain circumstances by the state, debt free. It will be sound money and just as desirable and as free from every
kind of inflationary tendency as the finest money that can be borrowed from the strongest bank on the face of the earth.
The question will be raised now as to how the money can be created. All that it is necessary to remember is that it will simply be a ticket to goods. Where goods are, tickets can be created. Where you have seats in a theatre, tickets to the seats can be created. Where there are seats in a train, tickets to those seats can be created. Where there are goods and services not being purchased by the purchasing power at present in circulation in the country, the government can create tickets representing those goods and services. Those tickets will be sound money and will not cause any rise in price, and consequently they will not cause any kind or degree of inflation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can they be cancelled?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Under certain circumstances they could be cancelled. I do not want to go into details, but that is a very good question that has been asked. I simply ask hon. members to bear in mind that in a talk of this kind it is not desirable to go into too great detail, not because I cannot do it but because, as I pointed out on March 7, in a talk of this kind it would make too long and complicated a speech if I went into too great detail.
In certain circumstances these tickets could be cancelled just as tickets to seats can be cancelled out of circulation. Under certain circumstances the banks lend great quantities of money. Under other circumstances they withdraw their loans and cancel the money out of circulation. The objection to the present system is that the money lent is not always lent upon sound principles nor is the cancellation of money out of existence always sound. That is why in the depression in the United States it was found that that country which had started with $23 billion found itself $8 billion short inside of four years, because $8 billion out of $23 billion of the purchasing power had been cancelled out of circulation. The United States was trying to carry on with too little money, and consequently it suffered just as much as an animal would suffer that had lost one-third of its blood.
Money can be cancelled out of circulation and would be under certain circumstances and in accordance with certain definite rules. I feel that I have said enough on this occasion to put before the house and before those in the country who are interested the social credit attitude on controls. Once more let me sum up. The Social Credit party is absolutely in favour of control by inducement, but it is
Emergency Powers

unalterably opposed to control by coercion, unless by some chance you had to deal with some pugnacious company and I doubt whether any such company would continue to carry on very long in the country. Social credit is opposed to autocratic and totalitarian control, but it is in favour of control that will control prices and wages by inducement, mainly by subsidies and bonuses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a very interesting exposition tonight on the theories of social credit, one which has been a little clearer than others I have heard and yet one which I think is based upon a false premise. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) state that he and his party agree that the cost of living must not be permitted to rise, but I cannot see how the cost of living can be kept down by inducement. I think it can be kept down only by the sanction of law or by the force of the state. An hon. MEMBER: How about subsidies? Mr. STEWART (Winnipeg North):	I
intended to deal with subsidies. I know in the province from which I come the price of milk was kept down by the provincial authorities, by the state if you like, despite the subsidy which was being paid. What intrigued me was the reference made by the hon. member to the United States, one which has been repeated in other parts of this house. I have heard the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) use it. The United States has been held up to us as an example of private enterprise. I think those who hold up the United States as an example of private enterprise have not delved deeply into the recent economic history of that country.
I would suggest to those who believe that the United States is the last hope of private enterprise that they read the minutes of the temporary national economic committee which was set up by the late President Roosevelt in 1938 and which made its report in 1942. The best statement I have seen about the last island of private enterprise appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 31 of this year. That paper eaidl:
Private enterprise, then, in its most complete form is to be found in a small island upon this continent.
Of course the largest part of that island is the LTnited States. I should like to examine the private enterprise which prevails in that country. All the figures I am using are those which have been submitted to that government committee, T.N.E.C. and all can be verified from the reports of that committee.

We find, for instance, that private enterprise may exist in the United States, but it is a private enterprise which is leading to a still greater concentration of economic power, a private enterprise which is leading increasingly to monopoly, and that, of course, belies the very meaning of private enterprise. Between 1938 and 1942, in 95 per cent of American industries, and those the smallest, employment declined by 23 per cent, whereas in the other five per cent, and those the largest corporations, employment increased by 22 per cent, showing a concentration of employment in the larger companies. From that we can deduce that the relative importance of small business is steadily declining, while domination by big business is becoming much more pronounced. Those figures are pointed by this interesting fact, that 50 per cent, or the smaller half of employers in the United States employed only four per cent of the labour in that country, while nine-tenths of one per cent of the largest employers employed 50 per cent of the wage-earners of the United States. These figures are startling in their implications, but I have checked them and rechecked them to make certain they are correct.
Some twelve years ago, in 1935, there was a study produced by the Brookings institution, one which involved the publication of four volumes, and those who were engaged in that study were not men who were notoriously sympathetic to the left in their outlook. One of the conclusions they came to was that in that land of free private enterprise the distribution of incomes amongst consumers was startlingly unequal and, to add point to that, we find from the T.N.E.C. report that one-tenth of one per cent of the richest families in the United States received as much income as did the lowest 42 per cent of the families in that country; surely another indication of the fact that wealth is becoming more and more concentrated in this last island of free and private enterprise.
Furthermore, those who were responsible for the Brookings study stated, what I hope we already know, that money savings did not automatically become new investments. As a result of that, there was a deficiency of purchasing power on the part of consumers. Those who had the money were unwilling either to spend it all in consumer goods or to risk it in new investment, so that there appeared on the economic scene in the United States an actual deficiency of purchasing power, which, of course, resulted in the depression.

Emergency Powers
What was the cost of that depression brought on by private enterprise? Between the years 1929 and 1939, 43 million man-years were lost through unemployment. This was private enterprise, perhaps not at its best, but private enterprise as it is expected to function again in the near future in the United States. Along with that loss in labour there was a loss, it has been calculated, of $120 billion in wages and in salaries, and during those eleven years when 43 million man-years were lost through unemployment the federal government had to spend between two and six billion dollars each year to alleviate hunger and suffering.
The hon. member who has just spoken has just told us that private enterprise has not failed. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that private enterprise has failed and for this reason if for none other, that private enterprise has never been able to give full employment to the people except in time of war. That is too expensive a way to provide full employment.
Another fact which that committee pointed out was that during the time it was sitting less than three per cent of United States families received incomes of $5,000 or more, while 54 per cent of the families received incomes of SI,250 or less.

speechtext: That is more than they get in Russia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have no doubt about that. It is also more than many get in Canada.
In 1935, based on reports of 400,000 corporations which filed balance sheets with the bureau of internal revenue, 55 per cent of these corporations held only 1-4 per cent of the total recorded assets, while two-tenths of one per cent, or, in number, 7S0 corporations, held 52 per cent of the recorded assets; thus showing once again the truth of what we have been saying, that private enterprise leads inevitably to the concentration of economic power and to monopoly. Indeed in 1941 one-half of one per cent of all manufacturing establishments were awarded 75 per cent of all war contracts. Thus, when we hear the United States praised as the home of private enterprise we should be careful how we accept those words, because private enterprise there is becoming more and more monopolistic enterprise. The odd thing is that most defenders of private enterprise assume without much reason, that the existing system is competitive and that competition in itself leads of necessity to efficiency. That was a theory which was held by Liberal economists
and Liberal philosophers over a hundred years ago. They believed that if there were many small units manufacturing, producing and distributing, the consumer would inevitably get the benefit. But the small manufacturing concerns found that competition was expensive and extravagant, and so we saw the more powerful ones gobbling up or driving into bankruptcy or absorbing their competitors until we have come to the system of free enterprise as it exists today.
Walter Lippmann, who is becoming more conservative as days go by, has this definition:
Competition is something of which producers have only as much as they cannot eliminate.
That, I think, is true. We find that same lack of competition in this country. We find that the people are being subjected not to the control of government but to the control of private enterprise. As a result of the price spreads commission, certain facts were brought to light, and we found this situation in Canada. I have here a table which I have taken from "The Control of Competition in Canada'' by Lloyd G. Reynolds. The table is headed, "Control of output in selected manufacturing industries," and it shows that 89 per cent of the output of automobiles is controlled by three firms; 100 per cent of the output of ammunition, explosive^, ammonia and chlorine is controlled by one firm; 75 per cent of the output of agricultural implements is controlled by four firms; 90 per cent of the output of cement is controlled by one firm; 93 per cent of the output of copper is controlled by four firms; 83 per cent of the output of canning (fruit and vegetable) is controlled by two firms; 79 per cent of the output of cotton yarn and cloth is controlled by three firms; 100 per cent of the output of electrical equipment is controlled by three firms; 91 per cent of the output of lead is controlled by one firm; 85 per cent of the meat packing is controlled by two firms; 100 per cent of the output of artificial silk is controlled by two firms, and so on all down the line. Private enterprise as it exists in the imagination of many members of this house does not exist in fact.
At this stage I should like to read from Hansard of 1932-33 certain remarks made by the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). At page 2510 he said:
Price fixing by agreements restrict and hamper trade internally.
Tlie internal trade of our country has become honeycombed and enmeshed by secret understandings and agreements. The protective tariffs, as they obtain in Canada today, have fostered the formation of combines, monopolies
Emergency Powers

and trusts, and under these combines, monopolies and trusts there are no end of secret agreements by which prices are being held at artificial figures.
The right hon. gentleman who made that statement is now Prime Minister of Canada, but we are still enmeshed and honeycombed with secret understandings and agreements, and many of them have been exposed on the floor of this house. And protective tariffs as they then obtained in Canada obtain in Canada today. The Prime Minister went on to say:
The system of distribution of products needs overhauling. Distribution should be on a service-at-cost basis. The spread in prices is too great, as any comparison of prices paid to producers with prices consumers have to pay will make self-evident.
That was true in 1933 and it is equally true today. The spread in prices today is too great; the spread in profits is too great. But lest I be accused of unfairness in quoting from only one section of the house, I will also quote from a radio address given on January 11, 1935, by one who was then leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Bennett. The title of this part of the address is the "Duty of the State". Here are Mr. Bennett's words, and we realize, after hearing them, why he had to find sanctuary in England:
In some ways, though only in some ways, conditions have improved since early times. Who made them better? Why, the state. In the past, even Liberal governments, now and then, in times of crises, had to swallow their economic principles and come to the rescue of the people. Laissez-faire had worked such frightful hardships in the circumstances that even the apostles of laissez-faire had to take note of that. But what a feeble, halting intervention. Now today, the accumulated inequalities of capitalism demand independent and courageous action by government. Is the party of laissez-faire ready to take itThe tragedy of these times has put that question straight up to it. Why has it not answered? I will tell you. Because it cannot say "Yes." Because it dare not say "No!" That is why it is dumb.
That is why the party of laissez-faire apparently finds itself in the same predicament today when on the subject of controls it cannot say "yes" and it dare not say "no."
The unfortunate thing about decontrol is that every step the government has taken has merely hastened the next step, and what a few months ago was called by this government orderly decontrol has now most obviously become a disorderly rout. We know what the effects of rising prices are. One would think the government especially would know. For their edification, I should like to read some more remarks by one who was then Minister

of Labour and who is now Prime Minister of Canada, 'remarks made as long ago as 1909 about the evils of rising prices:
This increase in the cost of living has not been confined to any one class. Rich and poor alike have had some experience of it, but it has had a very serious effect upon men of limited incomes, upon the wage-earning classes, upon those whose salaries are fixed and those who do not receive much in the way of remuneration.
What was true in 1909 is just as true today. To continue:
To one family after another it has meant curtailment of enjoyment, the forgoing of opportunities of education or recreation, a neglect of future needs, and the claims of others for future support, the giving up of insurance policies; to many it has meant a mode of living less congenial or beneficial to that previously enjoyed to some, downright privation and hardship; to all sacrifices of one kind or another.
These words were uttered thirty-seven years ago. They are equally true today, and I hope the government will pay some attention to the views of its present leader in this respect.
We have pointed out several times the experience of the United States. Last year, in June, OPA was killed. Immediately prices rose. Then there was a temporary recession, only to be followed by what has since turned out to be a constant increase in prices, as those who have been in the United States can well realize. In November of last year Mr. Donald Gordon, a man who has served Canada well and who has been frequently maligned, had this to say:
Canada now had an excellent opportunity to study the effects of general control removal in the Lfnited States before following a similar path.
We had an excellent opportunity to see the way, and we could have watched; we could have studied; but we refused to do so. The argument has been made that decontrol will lead eventually to increases in all sorts of goods on the market, but what do we find in the report of the wartime prices and trade board of last year at page 45? I am taking these two statements out of their context, but not unfairly. Dealing with furniture:
During the year, significant price adjustments were authorized on all the main types of furniture.
Later, on the same page:
By the end of the year, the total supply of household furniture had improved substantially. There was, however, a lack of balance in the supply since higher-priced lines W'ere quite plentiful and lower-priced lines w'ere often scarce or unobtainable.
That is what happened when control was taken off there. Naturally the manufacturers

Emergency Powers
went into more profitable lines, and the people not able to buy furniture are those who need it most.
There has been a general rise in prices all across the board and one which must have as its inevitable effect the lowering of the standard of living of Canadian workers; and, just as obviously, the trade union organizations of Canada are not going to permit that lowered standard of living to continue. Therefore they will demand, and I think rightly so, higher wages to maintain their standard of living, and so once again Canada is faced with the possibility if not the probability of severe labour troubles this year. But the government has continued its course of decontrol, having had some knowledge of what the people of Canada want. '
I think we can place a certain amount of faith in the Gallup poll, and the last Gallup poll I saw concerning the maintenance of controls led me to believe, properly, that two-thirds of the Canadian people wish to see these controls maintained. Had the government listened to the people more than to certain other advisers, I think these controls would have been maintained in better order than they have.
It has been argued frequently that by the imposition of controls our freedom in Canada is threatened. It all depends, of course, upon the definition of "freedom". Lincoln said that the sheep and the wolf were not agreed upon the definition of the word "freedom". I am quite sure that the hon. member for Stanstead and I, or the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and I are not agreed on the definition of that word. It appears to me that the freedom that they want is freedom for the economically powerful to continue to exploit the people. The freedom I should like to see is the freedom of the people maintained to continue a standard of living which will keep them in some measure of decency. But we are faced with the odd situation where those who are asking for freedom in Canada today are the top dogs and not the under dogs. There are the two conceptions of freedom: that, I think perhaps not unfairly, which is held by the hon. member for Stanstead of "Leave me alone; let me do as I want to do," that concept of freedom which gives all the power in the world to the powerful-
