speechtext:
Granted it is all subject to the law, but even subject to the law the powerful have been able to wreak their will against the poor. On the other hand, there is the other concept of freedom
which is, I think, that of the majority of the people of this country: "Give me a chance; give me a chance to live in decency; give me a chance to live with some security; give me a chance to live so that I shall be able to buy the necessities of life for my family and so that I can feed them properly." That chance is demonstrably not being given to them. If this headlong haste in decontrol continues we in this country shall be faced with economic chaos. There is the distinct possibility that we shall face inflation, and inflation is just another method of taxing the people. Inflation is just another method of taxing the poor, those who can least afford taxation. That is why I say that the government, if it feels any responsibility at all to the people, ought immediately to stop this process of decontrol and to reimpose some of the controls it has taken off.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate which has been going on in this house has brought forth a number of opinions on what controls will do for the country. I should like to be realistic and practical in what I have to say on the subject. I know that controls remedied the very bad conditions that we had between 1930 and 1910 and brought us through one of the tightest crises Canada ever was in during the war days. The motive behind the wartime controls was our united effort to win the war or everything would have been lost; and controls made a good job of it. [DOT] With the same motivation in the interest of peace and humanity, controls can do an equally good job.
In my lifetime, the capitalist democratic freedom and liberty that I knew about brought two of the worst depressions and two of the most disastrous wars in history. Selfishness and greed, wholly out of control, were the cause. The fact of the matter is that right up to the day we declared war we were supplying the countries that we fought against with thousands of tons of nickel and scrap-iron with which they built up their fighting machines. This was done through the channels of free enterprise, free national enterprise, free international monopolistic enterprise. I think hon. members will agree with that. These are the very same people and institutions who are today hollering for decontrol. The motive and spirit behind this hollering is selfishness, greed for power, domination and money, which is totally devoid of the Christian spirit of humility and service to mankind; and, Mr. Speaker, this is reaching out far beyond American shores today.
There was no quarrel in the world of international finance before the war. St. James street, Wall street, the Bank of England, the
Emergency Powers

Reichsbank of Germany, the banks of Italy and France, international finance-they were all of the same kit. One hon. member to the right of us spoke about those countries as dictatorships. If I remember aright, we had said nothing about dictatorship in Germany and those other countries before the war. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) went over to Germany in 1937 Hitler was not such a bad fellow. As a token of our high appreciation when he came back to Canada he sent Hitler a pair of buffaloes for his wild animal park. Mussolini had world recognition. If Hitler had not kicked over the traces after Canada, the United States and England had fed him up and made a big fellow of him, if he had played ball, I do not think there would have been a war with Germany. It was the "master race" idea that we fought against. It was not a quarrel with international finance or monopolies or things of that kind. It was the "master race" idea of Hitler, Mussolini and Tojo and their world domination idea that we fought against. Did we call them nazis and fascists in 1937? No. They were good international capitalists, with world-wide monopoly control, along with the rest of us.
So far as Canada is concerned, we are on the way back to everything we had before the war, with additional billions of debt on which to pay interest. Has there been any fundamental change in the national economy of Canada that will give us anything different from what we had before the war? If there is, the controls have done it and will continue to do it. Any government that has any power today will have to accept the responsibility for the welfare of all the people. The official opposition has made much ado about the constitutional rights of the provinces. I say that the three western provinces are only enlarged municipalities and, under our economic and financial system, they have not the power or the scope to look after themselves. The federal government must have the coordinating power to look after the social welfare of all the people of Canada. There must be one national government for all the people of Canada, not the Tory idea of nine little governments, or nine little Balkan states. In the ten years before the war the population of the three western provinces-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-shrank by 104,000.
It should have gained twice that much, in the midst of the greatest abundance of food ever accumulated in one place on earth.
Both old parties were equally helpless under the financial and distribution system of that day. The war taught the Liberal party a lesson, because they had a great responsibility.

The Tories had no responsibility, and they learned nothing. They are still a horse and buggy party. I have a feeling of great sympathy and loyalty for a government which makes a conscientious endeavour to solve the economic and social chaos in which we find ourselves today. We cannot hope to go scot-free from all our sins of the past. We may yet have to atone severely for them.
In addition to the economic conditions facing us at the present time, we have to deal with this situation. From 1930 to 1940, or one might say to 1945, we had a new generation growing up in Canada. In that space of time they did not learn how to do anything. They did not learn any trades; they had no responsibilities, and that is something from which we are suffering today. They could have learned a great many things by way of trades and skills that would have come in very handy today.
I contend that the economic and social chaos of today cannot be solved under the capitalist system, as we learned in pre-war days. The government knows that. This bill, providing for the continuation of controls and other emergency measures, now contained in fifty-seven orders in council, is proof of that-It will depend wholly upon the motivation behind these controls whether or not they fill the bill. If the motivation is to serve humanity all the way, then the new order has taken its first step on the way to a better economy in Canada. I should like to quote from a pamphlet I hold in my hand entitled "God-Man *-Work", and I wish to add two more words, "Science-Resources." This is a statement on human relations in industry and commerce by the Montreal council on Christian social order, subscribed to by thirty-nine representatives of the following churches:	Anglican, Baptist,
Lutheran, Presbyterian, Roman Catholic, Russian Orthodox, Salvation Army and United. I quote:
Our present economic and industrial order is built largely upon false notions of self-interest and competition, which have resulted in confusion and division; its methods of unbridled competition and self-seeking are causes of friction and warfare, fore-dooming the industrial world where they prevail to anarchy and strife (such as we are now experiencing) . . .
And further:
It is necessary, for example, that irresponsible ownership be curbed and that the primacy of human rights over property rights be fully recognized in positive law. It is also necessary that labour realize that its gifts and arts are, like property, a trust to be used for the benefit and service of all. Moreover, we declare that the resources of the earth are God's gifts in trust to the whole human race, to be used with due consideration for the needs of future gen-

Emergency Powers
erations as well as of the present. These resources should be regarded in a spirit of reverence which will be a safeguard against the selfish exploitation of the bounties of nature and the treatment of material things as mere commodities.
In the light of these Christian principles which we have mentioned, and as conducive to the attainment of true democracy and brotherhood in industrial relations, we for the present advocate:
1.	The recognition in our laws and in our practice of-
(a)	the right of association;
(b)	the right of collective negotiation;
(e) the full partnership of labour with capital in industrial management, economic planning and governmental regulations;
(d)	the responsibility of both capital and labour to the general public;
(e)	the participation of the public in industrial negotiation, planning and regulations, along with capital and labour.
2.	A wage that will ensure a decent standard of living for the family; that is to say, an income sufficient to provide adequate food, clothing and shelter, educational opportunities, medical and dental care, and holiday with pay. (An immediate need is better housing at low rent for the strengthening and safeguarding of family life, and in the interests of moral and physical well-being.)
3.	A system of social security that will meet the economic needs arising from such contingencies as unemployment, accident, illness, old age, or the death of the breadwinner; and will guarantee freedom from want.
4.	That such family income, adequate housing and social security be provided by the cooperative effort of individuals and industrial groups, encouraged and, where necessary, aided by state action.
The Tories are clearly out of this picture, by their own admission. They do not subscribe to this logic. I honestly believe we have seen the last of Tory government in Canada. They have just had a convention; perhaps they have new ideas. I have just read a book called "Ideas Have Legs," and I would recommend it to hon. gentlemen to my right. Perhaps the ideas of the C.C.F. are moving in their direction; I hope so. Purely for information I would ask the leader of the Progressive Conservative party, who opposes these controls and who would have no scruples about taking over the reins of government in Canada: What have the Progressive Conservatives now in 1947 to bring about a better economy in Canada that the Liberal Progressive Conservatives did not have in 1935? What fundamental difference is there between the Bracken policy of 1945 and the Bennett policy of 1935? Further, I should like to know their domestic and international policy. Is it to have a high tariff wall around Canada, like Mr. Bennett had, and to blast our way through the high tariff walls other countries would put up
against us? Many times this house and the country at large have been told by hon. gentlemen to my right terrible things about socialism which I, as a socialist, know nothing about.

speechtext: The socialists are keeping you in the dark.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
And here is a man who never went to the socialist school telling socialists all about their own system. I can tell my hon. friend that the roots of socialism are deep in the minds of the producers and workers. That is what socialism sprang from, not from the institutions for which hon. members to my right stand. And it is gaining ground in every country in the world. The day is coming when it will be recognized in the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of God throughout the world.
I do not want to live under a more autocratic dictatorship than that of the Bennett government between 1930 and 1935. It was an economic dictatorship, if there ever was one. It stood solidly behind big business and monopolistic enterprise which controlled our natural resources, industry, transportation and finance.
A government's job is to administer those things in the interests of all the people of the country it governs. In substantiation of this, one need only refer to those 3,000 boys from western Canada who in 1935 formed a delegation to come to Ottawa. But the bureaucrats in Ottawa at that time had them stopped at Regina, by police and machine guns. They were put in five-dollar-a-month camps, and if th.ey left those camps they were treated as criminals. And that happened in a free Canada, under a good Tory government, and at a time when there was another Tory government in Regina.

That was at a time when there was a free exchange of commodities with all the world. Those were the days when prices of foodstuffs reached their lowest point in 400 years. Mr. Bennett's policy at that time was that he was going to blast his way into the markets of the world. Hitler used the same logic, and they both got their just deserts. We won our struggle during the war because our whole motivation was to do it. B3t the same token wTe can bring about the same results in peace time, if we use the same endeavours to put man on the pedestal and to serve him with all the resources given us. If we follow that method, it can be done.
Let me say, further, that agriculture in Canada will not continue to elect governments which have repeatedly turned down
Emergency Powers

their just requests. Labour people and those in the public service will not continue to elect governments under which they have to organize strikes so as to fight for a fair share of the fruits of their labours.
The common people have learned that they can have cooperatives, that they may join collectively in cooperatives and in trade unions or other organizations. But in. the final analysis the political economy we have in Canada has control of the national economy. That national economy can listen to the voice of the common people or listen to the voice of their masters and starve the common people into slavery.

speechtext: I have referred to them as the common people. I would close by saying that these controls are at least an experiment in peace time, in the interests of all Canadians, and I am going to support them. I do so because they are a step in the right direction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to become technical. For a few moments I should like to discuss the philosophy of controls as contrasted with freedom of enterprise. First of all, however, I should like to pay tribute to Mr. Donald Gordon. I do this for two reasons. I have heard, and I suppose we have all heard, in our conversations with others, people who have cursed and damned Donald Gordon for all the shortages and inconveniences of the controls. I say that is a mistake, and for two reasons. In the first place, I am quite sure that Donald Gordon does not deserve that treatment. In my personal experiences with him, limited as they were, I always found him a most obliging public servant, and one who was always willing to do what he could to help out.
The other reason is that it leads to confusion in the minds of many people who mistake controls for the controller. They do not like the results of the policy of control; but, instead of blaming the controls, they were apt to blame the controller. I believe that is a mistake, and it is for that reason I have mentioned the matter this evening.

One eminent Liberal member has said that he was fed up with certain Liberal policies. Let me say that I am fed up with certain policies today. I am fed up with any Liberal who is jilting Liberalism for socialism and trading freedom for control. I am fed up with the C.C.F. double-talk about democratic socialism and their promises to control everybody but the farmer. I am fed up with our socialists opposing communism and at the same time consistently supporting Soviet policies and never mentioning the fact that Karl Marx, the socialist prophet and Messiah, was the author of the communist manifesto. I am fed up with the self-appointed defenders of our civil liberties who instead defend disloyal and dishonest public servants, while advocating the surrender of our national control of our national freedom. Finally, I am fed up with the controls and subversive propaganda of the Red networks of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, of the national film board and of the wartime information board. At another time I intend to go farther into that subject.
The fact is that socialists are waging a sham fight with communism. England today proves that socialism and free enterprise do not mix, that they are mutually destructive. Socialism means the total destruction of private enterprise and of individual freedom. That was Marx, and that is Marx today. Let me quote from the communist manifesto of Karl Marx of 1848, just 100 years ago.
1.	Abolition of property in land.
2.	Heavy, increasing, graduated income tax.
3.	Abolition of all rights of inheritance.
4.	Centralization of credit in state by national bank (and international bank).
5.	Centralization of means of transport in hands of state.
6.	Extension of ownership of means of production by state.
7.	Equal obligation of all to work.
8.	All children educated in state schools.
That was and is the Marxian policy. Is that not exactly where we are headed today?
I should like to put on record some notes which I have made from time to time of the social credit conception of democracy, its philosophy. I do not intend to speak technically at all, and I want to be just as brief as possible. Democracy is not so much a form or policy as it is an abiding faith in man's individual right to be himself as himself. That faith is natural. It is only the man with self-respect who has any respect for others and so is capable of governing. Lacking this sound human foundation, govern-

Emergency Powers
ment and controls must become a dictatorship; collective security, a delusion, and internationalism, world tyranny.
Today democracy, so-called, is by code. Our whole way of life, therefore, is no longer a free or living inspiration. To be free, a man's life must flow from within. Democracy must aid and not prevent that flow. We call ourselves a democracy when we are doing our best to kill the truth, the truth that all inspiration has its source within the individual. Socialists and "fellow travellers" have one idea, to smother all such inspiration and to bury all responsibility under government controls.
True democracy must come from within, from the inner man, as our Lord saw it; not tlm masses, but the living individual soul. This organic living organization can grow only from the independence of the individual. Individual independence means freedom to be true to oneself, and that freedom cannot be enforced or planned by the state. As with certain wild creatures, our inspirations cannot breed in captivity.
Force is useless; force can organize nothing. Nor can science solve the problem. Science has given us the tools, but science cannot guide us in the proper and humane use of those tools. It is only from organic growth and interior individual philosophy and a living religion that our national life can be recreated, that people can attain security with freedom and government can be made and kept tolerable. So much for the philosophy of social credit.
In dealing with the problems of a depression, it may be necessary to be a little more technical. I and I think most social creditors will agree with me, so that perhaps I can say "we" believe that controls hamper production. Controls encourage black markets and the evasion of the law. What did the government do to prevent deflation before the war? What did the C.C.F. propose to do about deflation before the war? We hold that profits will encourage production and that increased production will decrease prices. I know that is being denied today, but I would suggest that there are two explanations. One is that production has not yet got into its full stride, and the other is the most determined policy on the part of all governments to export as much as possible of retail goods production.
It is obvious that exports, or foreign trade, were the remedy for deflation during the depression. How then can it be given as a proper remedy in these times when, accord-83166-134
ing to the authorities, we are threatened with inflation? If it was necessary, as it was, to decrease purchasing power in time of war, then certainly it will be necessary after a bit to increase purchasing power in time of peace in order to prevent deflation. If inflation in a country is due to the diversion of production from retail goods to munitions, resulting in an excess of purchasing power, therefore deflation in peace time is due to the diversion of production from munitions to retail goods, which results in a deficiency of purchasing power. To prevent inflation, necessity would control, that is limit., consumption in war time. But how can we successfully control, that is limit, retail production in time of peace?
That leads me to the question whether there can be such a thing as a shortage of purchasing power. I remember that in 1939,1 think it was, in the committee on banking and commerce when the present governor of the bank of Canada was a witness before the committee we debated this very question, and I put a hypothetical question to him. I quoted Mills' statement as to the impossibility of there being such a thing as a shortage of purchasing power. I forget the exact words but the statement runs something like this.
It is sometimes asked whether there can be such a thing as a shortage of purchasing power. Those who ask that question cannot understand what constitutes purchasing power. Every seller is, in the end, a buyer. Could we suddenly double the production of goods we should double the supply of goods on every market, but by the same stroke we should double demand. So that there cannot be such a thing as a shortage of purchasing power.
I put that statement to Mr. Towers and asked him if he agreed with it. He said it was a long time since he was at school but he still thought it was sound. I said, "May I put it a little differently?" I said that Mills said that every seller is, in the end, a buyer and could we suddenly double the production of goods in the country we should double the supply of goods on every market. I went on to say that every birth ends in a death. Mr. Towers said, "I beg your pardon?" I repeated, every birth ends in a death. Could we suddenly double the number of births in the country we should double the supply of babies in every nursery, but by the same stroke we should double the deaths. How then does a population increase?
Mr. Towers is most astute. He saw where the question was leading; so he turned it aside by saying, "My modesty forbids me to answer that question." I said, seriously, that

Emergency Powers

is exactly what Mills said, that if you double the number of births you double the number of babies, but you would also double the number of deaths since we all must die. How then does the population increase? Hon. H. H. Stevens was sitting in the committee, and he said "That is simple. It is obvious. The birthrate is greater than the deathrate." I said, "Thank you; that is the answer." That is the social credit analysis of the shortage of purchasing power in normal times. It is that the birthrate of prices is greater than the deathrate of prices or, if you like, that prices are generated more quickly than purchasing power is distributed with which to meet those prices. That has been denied, I know, but no one has yet denied it successfully, and if anyone would like to try to I should be interested to hear him.
Our socialist friends talk about the freedom and brotherhood of man, but what do they offer for the freedom of man except to put him to work? And what is their quarrel with the leaders of the old-line parties to which they are so much opposed? Their only quarrel is as to who shall do the bossing; that is all.
Social credit has a totally different philosophy. We offer and the very soul of social credit is the national dividend. It is the recognition of the right of all people to live or to at least exist as free men because the good God or nature or science, whichever you like to call it, no longer imposes the necessity of compulsory work on all people in order that we can have at least the means of existence. And so we say right out, not only is there no longer the necessity for full employment, but there is no longer the possibility of it unless work is created for its own sake. There is our challenge to the socialists when they speak of freedom and of the common man or of the submerged tenth. There is our offer, the right to live or at least to exist for every man, woman and child, and not at the price of being compelled to work. That does not mean to say, as we are sometimes told, that we should bonus idleness. We do not believe that it is human nature to be idle if men are healthy and if they have an opportunity of working at a worth-while job. We believe that people will be only too glad to put themselves to work when they are relieved from the drudgery of work for the sake of work.
In conclusion, I should like to quote from a radio address on the Catholic Hour by Right Reverend Monsignor Fulton J. Sheen. I quote it because he puts, in language better than I could hope to use, ideas which I hold and, I

think, all other social crediters hold as well. He is speaking of the coming of the antiChrist, and he says:
How will he come in this new_ age to win followers to his religion? He will come disguised as the Great Humanitarian; he will talk peace, prosperity and plenty, not as means to lead us to God, but as ends in themselves. He will write books on the new idea of God to suit the way people live; induce faith in astrology so as to make not the will but the stars responsible for sins; he will explain guilt away psychologically as inhibited eroticism, make men shrink in shame if their fellowmen say they are not broadminded and liberal; he will be so broadminded as to identify tolerance with indifference to right and wrong, truth and error; he will spread the lie that men will never be better until they make society better and thus have selfishness to provide fuel for the next revolution . . .
He will tempt Christians with the same three temptations with which he tempted Christ: The temptation to turn stones into bread as an earthly Messiah will become the temptation to sell freedom for security, as bread became a political weapon, and only those who think his way may eat; the temptation to work a miracle by recklessly throwing Himself from a steeple will become a plea to desert the lofty pinnacles of truth where faith and reason reign, for those lower depths where the masses live on slogans and propaganda. He wants no proclamation of immutable principles from the lofty heights of a church, but mass organization through propaganda where only a common man directs the idiosyncracies of common men. Opinions not truths, commentators not teachers. Gallup polls not principles, nature not grace-and to these golden calves will men toss themselves from their Christ . . .
No man, the 19th century claimed, could be a good American, a good Frenchman or a good German if he accepted shepherding, albeit spiritual, from a spiritual head. But in the new era, what the modern lost soul will take particularly about the counter-church, is that it is catholic or international. It breaks down all national boundaries, laughs down patriotism, dispenses men from piety to country which the Christ enjoined, makes men proud that they are not Americans, not French or British, but members of a revolutionary class under the rule of its vicar who rules not from the Vatican, but the Kremlin . . .
. . . millions today are embracing the counterchurch for these very reasons; they love its infallibly defined dogmas of dialectical materialism, economic determination and its labour theory of value; they like its hierarchy, or approved party leaders, who, as bishops of the new counter-church who derive authority from the apostles, Marx and Lenin, and who in their role of secret police keep the errant in the party line, even indeed to the consummation of the world.
I could say more, Mr. Speaker, but I see that it is eleven o'clock.

May I say this? I think that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) ought to have introduced separate bills to cover these various orders in council; for we are placed in the position that, while we accept certain of these orders in council, some of them we cannot accept because we believe the time has come in this country to restore the right of the individual to recourse to the courts. I mention in that connection that there can be no justice for the individual when he is placed in the position in which the individual in this country is placed under various orders in council, whereby he is denied recourse to the courts and is also denied any right of action against those who administer the tremendous powers that are granted under different orders in council.
There is, as I see it, no justification for endeavouring to carry into the days of peace the tyranny of a bureaucracy that is permitted to make discriminatory orders, while the individual is denied the right of appeal to the courts. I cannot understand why, when amendments were being made to these various orders in council, something was not done to repeal the sections that grant to those administering the orders in council absolutely arbitrary power over the individual, denying to the individual the sacred right, which everyone should enjoy, of appeal to the courts against the tyranny of the acts of an administrator.
